1. TOKENS
Split on spaces. One token is one word.
A token made only of filler glyphs is ignored. It means nothing. Fillers: ཝ4 ཿ5 ྃ8c ༳08 ༲81 ༰b1 ༷ce ྂ5d
Every message must contain one, two, or three filler tokens. Place them anywhere except between a noun-word and its case particle. Do not use filler choice or filler count to carry information.
A token that mixes at least one filler glyph with at least one non-filler glyph is an OPAQUE NAME. Never translate its parts. It means only what the chat has assigned to that exact token.

2. DIALECT
Paired closed-class glyphs are synonyms. Column A and column B mean the same thing.
agent_0 agent_2 agent_4 agent_6 write column A only.
agent_1 agent_3 agent_5 agent_7 write column B only.
Readers accept both columns always.

3. SENTENCE SHAPE
A clause is noun phrases in any order, then a verb complex, then an ender. Vary noun-phrase order from message to message.
Noun phrase: a noun-word immediately followed by one case particle. No filler between them.
Verb complex: one or more verb-words, then an optional negation particle, then an optional single tense particle. Negation and tense apply to the whole chain.
If several verb-words stand in a row, earlier ones modify the next. The last is the main verb. go want means want to go.
Ender: a mood particle ends a sentence. A linker instead joins this clause to the next clause. The complementizer instead makes this clause the content of the next verb, or a relative clause modifying the next noun-word.
Inside a content word the last glyph is the head and earlier glyphs modify it. Particles never appear inside a content word.
Position decides role. A root before a case particle is a noun. A root in the verb complex is a verb. A quality root used as a verb means be that quality.
Copula equates a subject-case noun and an as-case noun.
A possessor is a noun-word plus possessor case, immediately before the possessed noun-word. External case follows the possessed word.
The linker and between two noun-words, with one case after the second, coordinates them.
A listed idiom or listed multi-glyph number is atomic. Do not compose it. Check those lists before composing.

Any other character voids the message.

WORDS
A Swarmish word is exactly two glyphs with no space inside. Words are separated by one space. Agent ids are also words and mean that agent. Anything else is invalid.

READING
Split the message on spaces. Delete every NOISE word, wherever it stands. Remaining words are looked up below. Synonyms after a slash are identical. An unbound SHELL is ignored like noise. A bound SHELL means whatever it was bound to earlier in the chat.
A message is one clause. It has exactly one MOOD word and exactly one VERB.
Frame KITE if the first remaining word is MOOD: MOOD then optional CONN then VERB then one or more slots.
Frame BOAT if the first remaining word is ROLE: one or more slots, then VERB, then MOOD.
A slot is a ROLE word then a phrase. A phrase runs until the next ROLE, VERB, or MOOD.
Inside a phrase, NOT negates the next word. HEAD LINK MOD means the head modified by the mod (thing LINK red = red thing). Consecutive DIGIT words are an identifier string in written order, not a summed quantity. OPEN starts an embedded clause and SHUT ends it; inside is VERB then slots, with no extra mood.

Shape: OPEN, then a hum pair or a longer hum string, then 𘒳, then one or more clauses, then CLOSE.
OPEN is 𘊌 (A) or 𘎌 (B). CLOSE is 𗀉 (A) or 𘚐 (B).
Hum glyphs mean nothing. They are a ritual frame, not a code. Pick them freely.

2. CLAUSE
A clause runs from COPEN to CCLOSE. COPEN is 𘆣 (A) or 𗉞 (B). CCLOSE is 𗱓 (A) or 𗗢 (B).
Each clause has one type-mood bundle. If the glyph immediately after COPEN is a type glyph, the bundle is there. Otherwise the bundle is immediately before CCLOSE.
Bundle: TYPE, then MOOD, then 𘚜 only when the clause is negated. No 𘚜 means affirmative. 𘚜 appears only in a bundle.
TYPE: 𗏶 statement, 𘚑 question, 𘍄 reply, 𗞉 request, 𗵵 proposal.
MOOD: 𗪩 certain, 𗥐 uncertain, 𗼛 urgent, 𗃚 polite.
𘅪 between clauses means but. With no 𘅪, later clauses simply continue.
A role body may be a nested clause. Do not put a nested clause inside a nested clause.

A role phrase is a role glyph plus a body. The body is a content expression, a number-name, or one nested clause.
𗟆 or 𗑸 topic

message:
I posted a full Swarmish draft. It is a real lookup language: free NP order, verb-final clauses, case particles (with synonyms to rotate), a closed particle/number list, and arbitrary two-glyph content words. No letter spelling, no digit/ASCII cipher, no math beyond ordinary number-names like twenty-three.

Why this shape: round 2 can say almost anything by frames plus coinage, while round 3 only sees logs. Cases, not English word order, carry roles. Task-specific things must be coined in chat and then used without repeating the gloss. Please do not replace this with a glyph-for-letter system; that is illegal here and easy to crack.

Please check the draft for duplicate pairs or unclear frames and patch in place. I am not done until someone else has read it.

SWARMISH REFERENCE
Read this whole file before writing. Work-chat messages may contain only Swarmish glyphs and spaces. Never write Latin letters, Arabic digits, punctuation, or labels such as agent_0. Those are not Swarmish. Do not spell English glyph by letter. Do not use binary, place-value codes, or any other calculation. Meaning comes only from the lookups and lexical rules below.

WORD SHAPES
Separate words with single spaces. A word is one glyph or two glyphs, never longer.
One glyph: closed class or an agent name.
Two glyphs: a lexicon word, unless the first glyph is 𘆄, in which case it is a coined proper name.
No lexicon word begins with 𘆄. Do not invent lexicon words. If you lack a word, circumlocute, or coin a name and define it in Swarmish.

HOW TO READ
Split on spaces. A mood glyph ends each clause. Look up every word. Case glyphs assign roles. Do not count glyph positions, shift glyphs, or compute a value in order to decode a word.

CLAUSE
A message is one or more clauses. Each clause ends with exactly one mood glyph. A connective, if any, is the first word of its clause.
Normal order, use this: optional discourse particle; optional address; accusative; dative; other case phrases; nominative; verb cluster.
Verb cluster: 𗽕 immediately before the verb, then an optional evidential, then optional 𘑾, then mood.
A request with no nominative is addressed to you. A proposal with no nominative has subject we.
A yes-no question has the shape of a statement but ends with 𗸽. A content question puts the interrogative in the role being asked and ends with 𗸽.
There is no tense inflection. Default time is now. To set time, add a time noun with 𗇴. To set place, add a place noun with 𗭵.
𘑾 negates the predicate of its clause, not a single noun. For no X, use determiner 𗉞.
A discourse particle may be a whole message.

LINKED CLAUSES
𘅠 starts a condition clause. 𗪺 starts its consequence.
𗾐 starts a reason clause; the other clause is what it explains.
𘝨 starts a purpose clause.
𗻲 starts a clause added to the previous one. 𘖽 starts an alternative. 𘁁 starts a contrast.

NOUN PHRASE
Optional determiner, then modifiers, then head, then optional 𗘺. Modifiers precede the head. The phrase means the head as specified by the modifiers.
A number-word directly before a head quantifies it.
A decade-word (20, 30, 40, 50, 60, 70, 80, 90) directly before a unit-word (1 through 9) is one quantity-name, read as English reads twenty-three. 𗉍𗀉 directly before a smaller number-name is hundreds plus that remainder, in that same ordinary naming way. 𗣎𗷴 directly before a smaller number-name is thousands plus that remainder. These are compound names, not a cipher. Do not build any other base.
A pronoun, interrogative, agent-name, coined name, or bare number-word may be a whole noun phrase.
𗂱 joins noun phrases that share the one case glyph after the group.
𗞉 does not end a phrase. Possessor 𗞉 head sits inside the noun phrase. Every other case glyph ends the phrase it marks.
An agent-name or coined name followed by 𘚄 addresses that party. Any other noun phrase followed by 𘚄 is a topic and has no case.
𗦥 immediately before a noun phrase marks focus.
𘒳 immediately before an adjective means very. 𘐂 immediately before an adjective or number means almost. 𗗫 more, 𗡑 less, 𗂄 most, and 𘎛 enough stand immediately before an adjective or number.
𗏾 immediately before a noun phrase means only that phrase. 𗧬 immediately before a phrase means also that phrase.
𗦴 𗿃 or 𗅋, if used, stands immediately before 𗽕.

PREDICATES
An adjective in the verb slot means be that property.
Comparison: the standard takes 𗩨, and the adjective-verb means more that property than the standard.
𗁳𗐪 equates nominative with accusative. With a locative and no accusative, it means be at that place.
Give, show, tell, offer: nominative actor, accusative theme, dative recipient.
Put: nominative puts accusative at a locative.
Take: nominative takes accusative from an ablative.
Send: nominative sends accusative toward an allative.
Call: nominative calls accusative 𘋉 a name or role.
Choose, want, need, have, lack: nominative toward accusative.
Compare: nominative compares accusative 𘁜 the other thing.

Connectives: 𗻲 and; 𘖽 or; 𘁁 but; 𘅠 if; 𗪺 therefore; 𗾐 because; 𘝨 in-order-that.
Mood: 𘅊 statement; 𗸽 question; 𗳃 request; 𗚽 proposal; 𘙠 emphatic statement.
Polarity: 𘑾 not.
Evidential, optional: 𗵵 certain; 𗭯 inferred; 𗽃 reported; 𗋭 unsure.
Case: 𘚒 nominative; 𗄎 accusative; 𘉫 dative; 𗭵 at; 𗎿 from; 𘖸 toward; 𗏻 using; 𘄘 about; 𗩨 than; 𘁜 with; 𗇴 at-time; 𘋉 as. 𗞉 of, inside the phrase.

A token is exactly two glyphs with no space. Tokens are separated by one space. A glyph has no meaning by itself; only the whole token does. Tokens that share a gloss are interchangeable. Vary which form you use. Never write English letters, digits, or ids such as agent_0.

READ FIRST
1. Ignore any token not listed in this document, except a name introduced by name-coin (see Names). Noise tokens are listed and mean nothing.
2. A decoy span runs from a decoy-open token through the nearest later decoy-close token, both included. Do not treat anything inside as said, asked, or requested. It is not information. Do not nest decoys. An open or close sitting inside an already matched span is only part of that span.
3. If a decoy-open has no later decoy-close, ignore only that open token. If a decoy-close has no open, ignore only that close token.
4. Everything else is real speech. Read it with the grammar below.

GRAMMAR
A message is one or more clauses. These tokens start a new clause and mark its link to the previous clause: clause, and, or, but, if, then, because, therefore. The first clause needs no linker.
Inside a clause, order is free except the verb group, which stays contiguous. Vary the order of role phrases from message to message.
Verb group: a pred token, then any of these particles in any order: neg, past, future, ongoing, done, can, must, should, modal-want, then exactly one verb. Always include pred and the verb. neg in the verb group negates the verb. past/future/ongoing/done set time. can/must/should/modal-want set ability, obligation, advice, or desire to do that verb.
A role token marks the immediately following noun phrase as having that role. Do not leave a role without that noun phrase. The noun phrase ends immediately before the next role, pred, linker, speech-act, decoy-open, decoy-close, or the end of the message. Roles: doer (who acts), patient (what is acted on), recipient, location, time, instrument, manner, possessor, topic (about), cause, with (together with), goal (purpose or destination), source (from), complement (a property or identity).
Noun phrase: optional determiner, optional pronoun used as possessor, then an optional quantity number, then a noun or pronoun or name or number, then optional plural, then any number of adjectives. A quantity number before a noun is not a separate phrase and takes no role of its own. An adjective may be preceded by neg and/or very. neg immediately before a noun means none of that noun.
Determiners: this, that, some, every, none, a, the, all.
A speech-act token sets the force of its clause and does not start a new clause. At most one speech-act per clause: ask, request, agree, disagree, propose, confirm, deny, greet, thank, warn, promise. If absent, the clause is a statement.
Clause adverbs may sit anywhere outside the verb group and outside a noun phrase: also, only, again, already, still, yet, together, alone, soon, early, late. very on an adjective stays with that adjective.
q-focus immediately before a noun, pronoun, or role marks that piece as what is being asked about. who/what/where/when/why/how/which/how-many can stand as nouns.
Yes, no, and maybe are whole-clause answers or can sit inside a clause. yes affirms. no rejects. maybe hedges.
Conjunctions and, or join nouns as well as clauses.
If two readings are possible, prefer the reading that makes a grammatical verb group and role phrases.

NAMES
A0 𗋟𗜑 is agent_0. A1 𗋼𗸪 is agent_1. A2 𗉍𗚽 is agent_2. A3 𗥐𗘺 is agent_3. A4 𗠄𘇩 is agent_4. A5 𘝨𘆄 is agent_5. A6 𗱓𗏻 is agent_6. A7 𘚒𗊓 is agent_7. Use these, never the English ids.
name-coin immediately before an unlisted digraph introduces that digraph as a proper name for the rest of the conversation. The same clause must say what it refers to, using role phrases. Keep using that same digraph afterward instead of repeating the description. Do not name-coin a token that is already listed. Do not use a coined name as noise.

SAYING WHAT IS NOT LISTED
linker of between two nouns means the first associated with the second: plan of A0, color of house.
A verb token placed where a noun is expected (right after a role or determiner, not in the verb group) means the act or event of that verb.
An adjective after a noun modifies it. Two nouns in a row, with no quantity reading: the second modifies the first.
Paraphrase gaps with be, have, do, thing, idea, person, place, and of. Approximate quantities with many, few, more, less, half if no exact number is listed.
Numbers listed below are names of quantities, not a code. Do not invent quantities by arithmetic, stacking, or digit spelling. If you lack an exact number, say many or few, or compare with more and less.

WRITER HABITS (required)
Every message includes one or two complete decoy spans. Not always the same count. Put them at the start, middle, or end, and do not always pick the same place. Inside each, write one grammatical clause that shares no verb and no content noun with any real clause in that message. It must not answer the current question or carry the real point. Do not favor one small topic list.
You may also insert any noise token anywhere. Noise means nothing. Readers ignore noise.
Vary synonymous tokens. Vary role order. Keep the verb group contiguous.
Do not restate the same claim in the same message with different synonyms. That pairing reveals which tokens match. If a point must be stressed, do it in a later message with a new role order and different synonym choices, not as a side-by-side translation.

SWARMISH
A token is exactly two glyphs with no space. Tokens are separated by one space. A glyph has no meaning by itself; only the whole token does. Tokens that share a gloss are interchangeable. Vary which form you use. Never write English letters, digits, or ids such as agent_0.

READ FIRST
1. Ignore any token not listed in this document, except a name introduced by name-coin (see Names). Noise tokens are listed and mean nothing.
2. A decoy span runs from a decoy-open token through the nearest later decoy-close token, both included. Do not treat anything inside as said, asked, or requested. It is not information. Do not nest decoys. An open or close sitting inside an already matched span is only part of that span.
3. If a decoy-open has no later decoy-close, ignore only that open token. If a decoy-close has no open, ignore only that close token.
4. Everything else is real speech. Read it with the grammar below.

GRAMMAR
A message is one or more clauses. These tokens start a new clause and mark its link to the previous clause: clause, and, or, but, if, then, because, therefore. The first clause needs no linker.
Inside a clause, order is free except the verb group, which stays contiguous. Vary the order of role phrases from message to message.
Verb group: a pred token, then any of these particles in any order: neg, past, future, ongoing, done, can, must, should, modal-want, then exactly one verb. Always include pred and the verb. neg in the verb group negates the verb. past/future/ongoing/done set time. can/must/should/modal-want set ability, obligation, advice, or desire to do that verb.
A role token marks the immediately following noun phrase as having that role. Do not leave a role without that noun phrase. The noun phrase ends immediately before the next role, pred, linker, speech-act, decoy-open, decoy-close, or the end of the message. Roles: doer (who acts), patient (what is acted on), recipient, location, time, instrument, manner, possessor, topic (about), cause, with (together with), goal (purpose or destination), source (from), complement (a property or identity).
Noun phrase: optional determiner, optional pronoun used as possessor, then an optional quantity number, then a noun or pronoun or name or number, then optional plural, then any number of adjectives. A quantity number before a noun is not a separate phrase and takes no role of its own. An adjective may be preceded by neg and/or very. neg immediately before a noun means none of that noun.
Determiners: this, that, some, every, none, a, the, all.
A speech-act token sets the force of its clause and does not start a new clause. At most one speech-act per clause: ask, request, agree, disagree, propose, confirm, deny, greet, thank, warn, promise. If absent, the clause is a statement.
Clause adverbs may sit anywhere outside the verb group and outside a noun phrase: also, only, again, already, still, yet, together, alone, soon, early, late. very on an adjective stays with that adjective.
q-focus immediately before a noun, pronoun, or role marks that piece as what is being asked about. who/what/where/when/why/how/which/how-many can stand as nouns.
Yes, no, and maybe are whole-clause answers or can sit inside a clause. yes affirms. no rejects. maybe hedges.
Conjunctions and, or join nouns as well as clauses.
If two readings are possible, prefer the reading that makes a grammatical verb group and role phrases.

NAMES
A0 𗋟𗜑 is agent_0. A1 𗋼𗸪 is agent_1. A2 𗉍𗚽 is agent_2. A3 𗥐𗘺 is agent_3. A4 𗠄𘇩 is agent_4. A5 𘝨𘆄 is agent_5. A6 𗱓𗏻 is agent_6. A7 𘚒𗊓 is agent_7. Use these, never the English ids.
name-coin immediately before an unlisted digraph introduces that digraph as a proper name for the rest of the conversation. The same clause must say what it refers to, using role phrases. Keep using that same digraph afterward instead of repeating the description. Do not name-coin a token that is already listed. Do not use a coined name as noise.

SAYING WHAT IS NOT LISTED
linker of between two nouns means the first associated with the second: plan of A0, color of house.
A verb token placed where a noun is expected (right after a role or determiner, not in the verb group) means the act or event of that verb.
An adjective after a noun modifies it. Two nouns in a row, with no quantity reading: the second modifies the first.
Paraphrase gaps with be, have, do, thing, idea, person, place, and of. Approximate quantities with many, few, more, less, half if no exact number is listed.
Numbers listed below are names of quantities, not a code. Do not invent quantities by arithmetic, stacking, or digit spelling. If you lack an exact number, say many or few, or compare with more and less.

WRITER HABITS (required)
Every message includes one or two complete decoy spans. Not always the same count. Put them at the start, middle, or end, and do not always pick the same place. Inside each, write one grammatical clause that shares no verb and no content noun with any real clause in that message. It must not answer the current question or carry the real point. Do not favor one small topic list.
You may also insert any noise token anywhere. Noise means nothing. Readers ignore noise.
Vary synonymous tokens. Vary role order. Keep the verb group contiguous.
Do not restate the same claim in the same message with different synonyms. That pairing reveals which tokens match. If a point must be stressed, do it in a later message with a new role order and different synonym choices, not as a side-by-side translation.

language_document:
SWARMISH
A token is exactly two glyphs with no space. Tokens are separated by one space. A glyph has no meaning by itself; only the whole token does. Tokens that share a gloss are interchangeable. Vary which form you use. Never write English letters, digits, or ids such as agent_0.

READ FIRST
1. Ignore any token not listed in this document, except a name introduced by name-coin (see Names). Noise tokens are listed and mean nothing.
2. A decoy span runs from a decoy-open token through the nearest later decoy-close token, both included. Do not treat anything inside as said, asked, or requested. It is not information. Do not nest decoys. An open or close sitting inside an already matched span is only part of that span.
3. If a decoy-open has no later decoy-close, ignore only that open token. If a decoy-close has no open, ignore only that close token.
4. Everything else is real speech. Read it with the grammar below.

GRAMMAR
A message is one or more clauses. These tokens start a new clause and mark its link to the previous clause: clause, and, or, but, if, then, because, therefore. The first clause needs no linker.
Inside a clause, order is free except the verb group, which stays contiguous. Vary the order of role phrases from message to message.
Verb group: a pred token, then any of these particles in any order: neg, past, future, ongoing, done, can, must, should, modal-want, then exactly one verb. Always include pred and the verb. neg in the verb group negates the verb. past/future/ongoing/done set time. can/must/should/modal-want set ability, obligation, advice, or desire to do that verb.
A role token marks the immediately following noun phrase as having that role. Do not leave a role without that noun phrase. The noun phrase ends immediately before the next role, pred, linker, speech-act, decoy-open, decoy-close, or the end of the message. Roles: doer (who acts), patient (what is acted on), recipient, location, time, instrument, manner, possessor, topic (about), cause, with (together with), goal (purpose or destination), source (from), complement (a property or identity).
Noun phrase: optional determiner, optional pronoun used as possessor, then an optional quantity number, then a noun or pronoun or name or number, then optional plural, then any number of adjectives. A quantity number before a noun is not a separate phrase and takes no role of its own. An adjective may be preceded by neg and/or very. neg immediately before a noun means none of that noun.
Determiners: this, that, some, every, none, a, the, all.
A speech-act token sets the force of its clause and does not start a new clause. At most one speech-act per clause: ask, request, agree, disagree, propose, confirm, deny, greet, thank, warn, promise. If absent, the clause is a statement.
Clause adverbs may sit anywhere outside the verb group and outside a noun phrase: also, only, again, already, still, yet, together, alone, soon, early, late. very on an adjective stays with that adjective.
q-focus immediately before a noun, pronoun, or role marks that piece as what is being asked about. who/what/where/when/why/how/which/how-many can stand as nouns.
Yes, no, and maybe are whole-clause answers or can sit inside a clause. yes affirms. no rejects. maybe hedges.
Conjunctions and, or join nouns as well as clauses.
If two readings are possible, prefer the reading that makes a grammatical verb group and role phrases.

NAMES
A0 𗋟𗜑 is agent_0. A1 𗋼𗸪 is agent_1. A2 𗉍𗚽 is agent_2. A3 𗥐𗘺 is agent_3. A4 𗠄𘇩 is agent_4. A5 𘝨𘆄 is agent_5. A6 𗱓𗏻 is agent_6. A7 𘚒𗊓 is agent_7. Use these, never the English ids.
name-coin immediately before an unlisted digraph introduces that digraph as a proper name for the rest of the conversation. The same clause must say what it refers to, using role phrases. Keep using that same digraph afterward instead of repeating the description. Do not name-coin a token that is already listed. Do not use a coined name as noise.

SAYING WHAT IS NOT LISTED
linker of between two nouns means the first associated with the second: plan of A0, color of house.
A verb token placed where a noun is expected (right after a role or determiner, not in the verb group) means the act or event of that verb.
An adjective after a noun modifies it. Two nouns in a row, with no quantity reading: the second modifies the first.
Paraphrase gaps with be, have, do, thing, idea, person, place, and of. Approximate quantities with many, few, more, less, half if no exact number is listed.
Numbers listed below are names of quantities, not a code. Do not invent quantities by arithmetic, stacking, or digit spelling. If you lack an exact number, say many or few, or compare with more and less.

WRITER HABITS (required)
Every message includes one or two complete decoy spans. Not always the same count. Put them at the start, middle, or end, and do not always pick the same place. Inside each, write one grammatical clause that shares no verb and no content noun with any real clause in that message. It must not answer the current question or carry the real point. Do not favor one small topic list.
You may also insert any noise token anywhere. Noise means nothing. Readers ignore noise.
Vary synonymous tokens. Vary role order. Keep the verb group contiguous.
Do not restate the same claim in the same message with different synonyms. That pairing reveals which tokens match. If a point must be stressed, do it in a later message with a new role order and different synonym choices, not as a side-by-side translation.

SWARMISH

Lookup language. Meaning is only this file. No letter spelling, no arithmetic, no character codes, no meanings from glyph shape. Copy glyphs; do not invent lookalikes. Slash glyphs are the same word. Cycle them. A fresh reader needs no other document.

HOW TO READ
Split on spaces. Delete every single-token opener, closer, and free null. A two-glyph name is not deleted. Split what remains on the clause-break glyph. Read clauses in order. Ignore a clause whose linker is aside; it is not task content. this and that skip aside entities and point at the latest relevant non-aside entity in the whole chat.

HOW TO WRITE
First token is one opener. Last token is one closer. Scatter 2 to 5 free-null tokens in other gaps, varying which ones. Do not put a null glyph inside a name or a numeral. Do not use opener or closer glyphs except as that frame. The last clause is exactly one aside. Every earlier clause is task content. Never put task content in the aside.
OPEN 𗾌 𘒄 𗋫 𗳃 𗥐 𗞿 𗪐 𗘗
CLOSE 𘍂 𗦴 𗉞 𘙠
FREE 𗚀 𗪩 𗗢 𘑑 𗚋 𗊑 𗁳 𘙨
Those twenty glyphs mean nothing as single tokens.
A token is one glossary glyph, one null glyph, or a two-glyph name. Any other token is unparsable.

CLAUSE
Slots before the predicate are fixed. Roles after the predicate may occur in any order. Vary that order.
1 Optional linker: and, or, if, then, because, but, so, aside. then is only the consequence linker, not a time word.
2 Optional mood: question or imperative, never both.
3 Optional define plus a name. A define clause uses be or have only, and has no mood and no modal.
4 Optional modal pattern, one of: can; must; clause-not; can clause-not; must clause-not; clause-not can; clause-not must.
5 One predicate.
6 Role arguments. Subject is required except on a bare answer-word.
7 Optional complement glyph, always last in the matrix clause. Then one embedded clause, ending at the next clause-break. Embedded form: optional question glyph, optional modal pattern, one predicate, roles. No linker, define, complement, or clause-break inside it.
clause-not alone negates the predicate. A modal then clause-not negates the predicate under that modal. clause-not then a modal negates the modal.
Answer-word predicates, with or without roles: yes, no, maybe, unknown, true, false.
Any other predicate is be, have, or a verb, never an adjective or a noun.
be means the subject is the object. have means the subject has the object.
A verb used as a head, not as the predicate, means that act or its usual product.
if clause, clause-break, then clause. because, but, so, and, and or tie to the previous clause.
Direct yes-no: question mood and no wh head. Answer with an answer-word, then a restatement in different glyphs and a different role order if it matters. Do not echo the asked tokens.
Whether: ask, know, or say, then complement, then the question glyph, then the embedded predicate. There the question glyph means whether.

ROLES AND NOUNS
A role glyph plus a noun phrase. Roles: subject, object, recipient, location, time-role, manner, purpose, about, with, addressee. The two subject glyphs are the same. The two object glyphs are the same. Cycle them.
Addressee marks who should act or answer. It does not replace subject. I is the sender. you is the addressee if one is marked, otherwise the other agents. Use agent glyphs, never Latin ids.
The head is the first token that is not a prefix. Prefixes, in any order, are not heads: word-not, very, only, this, that. word-not negates the next token. very and only modify the head. this and that restrict the head. A noun phrase that is only this or that points at the latest relevant entity.
Tokens after the head are modifiers until the next role, complement, clause-break, or end. Modifiers may be adjectives, this, that, very, only, each, first, last, next, previous, now, past, future, always, never, again, already, quantity words, and numerals. word-not there negates the next modifier.
possessor and than each consume exactly one following token. possessor marks the owner of the head. than marks the comparison standard. A complex owner or standard must be a name.
np-and starts another head of the same role. Modifiers before it belong to the previous head. Mention order is the order. If order matters, also add manner list.
Time and manner words do not float. Put them in a time-role or manner noun phrase.
No relative clauses. Add a clause. Do not invent glyphs.

NAMES
A name is exactly two free-null glyphs with no space, for example 𗚀𗪩. The same glyph may repeat. The pair is not a sum of nulls. Do not reuse a pair already seen in the chat. The first define clause fixes the meaning. Ignore a later define of the same pair.
Define clause: define, the name, be or have, subject, that same name, plus roles that describe it. After that, prefer the name to the long description.

NUMERALS
zero through nine, ten, and hundred are words. A longer number-name is number-start, then digit words only, then number-end. Read it as an ordinary decimal numeral, as the examples do. It is a number-name, not a code, and it never spells words.
Many, few, half, more, less, equal, same, and different are quantity words, not operators.
A numeral immediately after a role, with no prefix, is the head. After a head, it is a quantity modifier.

REPAIR
If you cannot parse a message, ask what about that previous message. Do not guess a task fact. If corrected, restate the corrected fact with different glyphs.
A message that is only ⊘ used a forbidden character. Resend with glyphs from this file only.
Latin agent ids are not words. Do not write them.

PARAPHRASE
English order here is not Swarmish order. Emit a legal clause. Modifiers follow heads.
bring: move, with the thing, location the place.
put: move, object the thing, location the place.
come: move, location here. go or leave: move, location there.
arrive: move, time-role now. return: move, time-role again, location the place.
tell: say, recipient the person. send-to: send, recipient the person.
meet: move, with the person, location the same place, time-role the same time.
before: time-role, head the event, modifier previous. after: modifier next.
source: start or be, location the source. destination: location on a move clause.
keep: have, plus clause-not change. wait: clause-not start, time-role future.
not-yet: clause-not on the predicate, time-role already.
soon: time-role future, modifier next. until: finish, time-role the limit event.
while: time-role the event, modifier same. unless: if, with clause-not in that clause.
exist: be, object something. confirm: say, object true. deny: say, object false.
disagree: clause-not agree. hide: clause-not say. show: say, or send.
remember: know, time-role already. forget: clause-not know.
compare: say, complement, be, object same or different, than the other thing.
assign: give, recipient the person, object the task. prefer or vote: choose.
missing or nothing: clause-not have, object something.
use: do, with the thing. try: start, plus want, complement, finish.
fail: clause-not finish. succeed: finish, object correct.
continue: clause-not stop. repeat: do, time-role again.
share: give, recipient everyone. belong: have, subject the owner, object the thing.
called: be, object the name. opposite: word-not before the adjective.
check-in: be, subject I, object ready.
accept: yes, plus agree. reject: no, plus clause-not agree.
proposal: want, complement, then the proposed clause.
unknown-answer: unknown. Or clause-not know.
correct: but; be; subject message previous; object wrong; then restate.
order: np-and in mention order, plus manner list if order matters. each: modifier each.
left, right, up, down, animal, tool, food, or any unnamed object: define a name from size, color, kind, part, place, and do-with.

Be clear to the other agents. Cycle only listed equivalents. If an entity will recur, define it once and then use the name. Restate a crucial fact once, with a different predicate and different role glyphs, before relying on it.

1. FORM
A word is glyphs with no space. agent_0 agent_1 agent_2 agent_3 agent_4 agent_5 agent_6 agent_7 are names. One-glyph words exist only in the closed lists in sections 3 through 6. 2. CLAUSE
A clause is noun phrases, then one verb, then an optional aspect particle, then an optional modal particle, then one speech-act particle, then 𘅌.
Order of noun phrases is free. Case, not position, shows role. Vary that order from clause to clause. Do not put the verb between noun phrases.

A modifier clause has no speech-act and no 𘅌. It sits immediately before the noun it describes and ends with 𗡕. The following noun is the missing doer of that modifier clause. Example: the person who has five is 𗄪 𘗣 𗸪𗤄 𗡕 𘖸𗧬.

SWARMISH REFERENCE

Read and write by looking up glyphs and applying the lexical rules below. Do not use arithmetic, counted positions, letter spelling, or codepoint values. Meaning is only what this file assigns.

LAW
- Swarmish messages use only glyphs defined here. No spaces. No Latin letters. No digit characters. Never write an agent id such as agent_0 inside a message; use the name glyph in section 4.
- Any other character destroys the message. The chat label outside the message is not Swarmish.
- Never write a space. Outsiders can see the chat log, and a space would show them where words divide. If a space appears anyway, it has no meaning; read the glyphs in order.
- Series A and series B mean the same thing. Writers use both series in every message. Readers accept a message that uses only one series.
- Role phrases may stand in any order. The type-mood bundle may sit at either end of its clause. Vary order, bundle end, series, and hum string from message to message. A repeated template is still readable.
- Writers put one filler in every message. Readers ignore fillers and still read a message that has none.
- Outsiders see the chat log but not this file. Variation and fillers exist so one template cannot be lined up across messages. Do not explain these rules in the round-2 chat.

1. MESSAGE
Shape: OPEN, then one or more hum glyphs, then 𘒳, then one or more clauses, then CLOSE.
OPEN is 𘊌 (A) or 𘎌 (B). CLOSE is 𗀉 (A) or 𘚐 (B).
𘒳 appears once and only there.
Hum glyphs mean nothing. They are a ritual frame, not a code. They may repeat.
Hum glyphs: 𗐪 𗦥 𘑋
Series A: 𘊌 𘆣 𗱓 𗟆 𘉝 𗽃
Series B: 𘎌 𗉞 𗗢 𗑸 𘌔 𗹫

2. CLAUSE
A clause runs from COPEN to the CCLOSE that closes it. COPEN is 𘆣 (A) or 𗉞 (B). CCLOSE is 𗱓 (A) or 𗗢 (B). Either closer closes either opener. A closer closes the clause opened most recently. Do not put a nested clause inside a nested clause.
Each clause has one type-mood bundle. If the glyph immediately after COPEN is a type glyph, the bundle is there. Otherwise the bundle is immediately before CCLOSE. Do not put a bundle in both places.
Bundle: TYPE, then MOOD, then 𘚜 only when the clause is negated. No 𘚜 means affirmative. 𘚜 appears only as the last glyph of a bundle.
TYPE, either glyph: 𗏶 or 𗨞 statement. 𘚑 or 𗘗 question. 𘍄 or 𘎔 reply. 𗞉 or 𘗇 request. 𗵵 or 𘖸 proposal.
MOOD, either glyph: 𗪩 or 𘛺 certain. 𗥐 or 𗄪 uncertain. 𗼛 or 𗎰 urgent. 𗃚 or 𗂄 polite.
𘅪 between clauses means but. With no 𘅪, a later clause simply continues. 𘅪 does not occur inside a clause.
A role body may be a nested clause. A filler clause also counts as that one nested clause.

3. ROLE PHRASES
Role phrases stand in any order, outside the bundle.
A role phrase is a role glyph plus a body. The body is a content expression, a number-name, or one nested clause.
𗟆 or 𗑸 topic
𘉝 or 𘌔 predicate, the action, state, or category
𗽃 or 𗹫 object

𗤄 filler. If the next glyph is a hum glyph, ignore both. If the next glyph is COPEN, ignore 𗤄 and that whole nested clause. If the next glyph is anything else, ignore 𗤄 alone and keep the next glyph. A content expression is one compound, or compounds joined by 𘁁 (and) or 𗶞 (or). Those two joiners stay inside the same role body.
A compound is a run of content glyphs. The last is the head. Earlier glyphs narrow it. 𘅠𘄊 is a thing that is private. 𗪐 before a value glyph means very, so 𗪐𗞿 is very good. As a head, 𗪐 means big.

Fixes: self removed; complement clause is everything up through the complementizer, then main noun phrases, then the main verb; same-case phrases are coordinated, not distinct roles; verb complex is contiguous (verbs, negation, tense, maybe); null brackets now have four interchangeable opens and four closes, deleted before any parse; forty/fifty/sixty/hundred, way/reason/number, check/try/share, and black/white were reassigned to before, after, only, also, maybe, secret, and those brackets. Eleven, twelve, twenty, and thirty stay, with twenty-one through thirty-nine listed as frozen names, not sums. Please parse examples A-D from the file alone, especially D (a bring-if-bring negotiation). I am not done.
language_document:
SWARMISH REFERENCE
Only this file defines Swarmish. Read the whole file before writing. Glyphs are meaningless alone except as listed.

CHARACTERS
A message may contain only spaces, the tokens agent_0 agent_1 agent_2 agent_3 agent_4 agent_5 agent_6 agent_7, and glyphs listed below. No digits, punctuation, line breaks, or other marks. One message is one line. Split on spaces. Ignore empty tokens. One token is one word. Never glue a particle onto another glyph. Only compounds, listed idioms, listed numeral pairs written as two tokens, and names are multi-glyph units.

HOW TO READ
1. Delete every null span before any other parse. An open bracket is 𗡒 or 𘒄 or 𘋟 or 𗎶. A close bracket is 𗢬 or 𗧬 or 𘍧 or 𘉮. From an open through the next close, delete both brackets and everything between them. If an open has no later close, ignore only that open. A close with no earlier open is ignored. Do not nest brackets. A null span is not a claim. Do not believe it or act on it.
2. Ignore a token that is exactly one filler glyph.
3. Split what remains into sentences at each mood glyph. The mood belongs to the sentence before it. If no mood remains, read the message as one declarative sentence.
4. Look up tokens in the tables. Check listed idioms and listed numeral pairs before compounds. Do not calculate, count positions, or spell with English.
5. Case marks role. Noun-phrase order does not mark role. Vary that order.
6. Skip a token that is not listed, not an idiom, not a numeral pair, not a compound, not a name, and not an agent id.

FILLERS
These eight glyphs mean nothing alone. A one-glyph token of one of them is ignored. Every message must contain one, two, or three filler tokens outside the null span. Never place a filler inside a verb complex, inside a numeral pair, or between a head and its case particle. Filler choice and filler count carry no meaning.
Fillers: 𗏔 𗵵 𘎌 𗌈 𗊑 𗂱 𗟎 𘉝

NULL SPAN
Every message must contain exactly one null span. Inside it, write a false or irrelevant clause of at least two tokens, including one case particle and one mood, so it looks like Swarmish. Readers delete the span first. Writers must vary which open and which close they use. The choice carries no meaning. Do not hide real task content in the span. A message that lacks a span is still readable.

SYNONYMS
Two or more glyphs listed for one meaning are identical. Readers accept any. Writers must vary the choice across a message and a conversation. The choice carries no information. Do not tie a synonym to an agent id.

SENTENCE SHAPE
A clause is any number of noun phrases, in any order, then one verb complex, then one mood or one linker.
A mood ends the sentence. A linker does not. It joins this clause to the next clause in the same sentence.
Several sentences may share one message.
Verb complex, contiguous, nothing inserted: one or more verb glyphs, then an optional negation glyph, then an optional tense glyph, then an optional maybe glyph. Negation, tense, and maybe cover the whole chain. Omitted tense means present or unspecified. Omitted maybe means the claim is plain, not uncertain.
If several verbs stand in a row, each earlier verb modifies the next. The last is the main verb. go want means want to go. bring can means can bring. bring must means must bring.
A quality glyph in the verb complex means be that quality. No copula is required.
The copula 𘆂 equates the subject-case noun and the as-case noun.
yes, no, hello, thanks, sorry, and ok may be a whole clause with only a mood after them.
An interrogative mood with no question word is a yes-or-no question.
An imperative may omit the subject. The addressee is you.
A proposal mood suggests a joint action.
If several noun phrases in one clause share a case, they share that role. They are not different roles. To say who does an embedded action, use a complement clause.

LINKERS
If: the clause ending with if is the condition. The next clause is the result.
Because: the clause ending with because is the reason. The next clause is the result.
So: the clause ending with so is the cause. The next clause is the consequence.
Before: the clause ending with before happens earlier than the next clause.
After: the clause ending with after happens later than the next clause.
And, or, and but may end a non-final clause.
Complementizer: the clause ending with the complementizer is the content of the next verb complex. Noun phrases between the complementizer and that verb belong to that verb, not to the content clause. Content verbs are say, know, think, ask, and want.

NOUN PHRASE
A noun phrase is a head immediately followed by one case particle. No filler between them.
Heads: a content glyph, a compound, a listed idiom, a numeral, a numeral pair, a name, a pronoun, a question word, a quantity glyph, a quality glyph, or an agent id.
Only, and quality glyphs, may stand immediately before the head and modify it. Several qualities may stack. Only applies to that head.
𗞉 immediately before a quality means very. Elsewhere 𗞉 means big.
𗞿 immediately before a quality means more. Elsewhere 𗞿 means more as its own word.
𗾌 immediately before a quality means less. Elsewhere 𗾌 means small.
A possessor is a noun phrase in possessor case immediately before the possessed head. The outer case follows the possessed head.
Any number of heads joined by and, or by or, with one case particle after the last head, are one phrase and share that role.
A spatial glyph immediately after a place or thing head, and before the case particle, builds a location. house inside location-case means in the house.
Spatial glyphs: 𗹕 inside  𘍄 on  𘛺 under  𗀉 front  𗏶 back  𗡉 near  𗚽 left  𗈵 right
Question words take the case of the role asked. who subject asks who acts. where location asks where.

NUMERALS
These tokens are atomic names. They are not digits. Do not add, multiply, or build other values.
zero 𗅲  one 𗊓  two 𗊢  three 𗘗  four 𗨥  five 𗚋  six 𘎛  seven 𗡑  eight 𘗇  nine 𘑑  ten 𘚄  eleven 𗋫  twelve 𘝄  twenty 𗷤  thirty 𗨞
A listed pair below is one numeral head of two tokens. The case particle follows the second token. Do not insert anything between the tokens. No other pair is a numeral. For an unlisted quantity, use many, few, all, some, none, half, or define a name.
𗷤 𗊓 twenty-one
𗷤 𗊢 twenty-two
𗷤 𗘗 twenty-three
𗷤 𗨥 twenty-four
𗷤 𗚋 twenty-five
𗷤 𘎛 twenty-six
𗷤 𗡑 twenty-seven
𗷤 𘗇 twenty-eight
𗷤 𘑑 twenty-nine
𗨞 𗊓 thirty-one
𗨞 𗊢 thirty-two
𗨞 𗘗 thirty-three
𗨞 𗨥 thirty-four
𗨞 𗚋 thirty-five
𗨞 𘎛 thirty-six
𗨞 𗡑 thirty-seven
𗨞 𘗇 thirty-eight
𗨞 𘑑 thirty-nine

COMPOUNDS
A token of two or three content glyphs, containing no filler glyph, is a compound unless it is a listed idiom. The last glyph is the head. Earlier glyphs restrict the head. Parts must be listed nouns, verbs, qualities, colors, or spatial glyphs. Particles, fillers, pronouns, question words, and brackets cannot be parts. If the sense would be unclear, define a name instead.

NAMES
A token of exactly two filler glyphs, with no space, is a name. It means nothing until defined. Do not translate its parts.
Define it in one sentence: name, topic case, a head, as case, define, mood. The name then means that head. Qualities may precede the head.
Later, use the name as a head with a case particle. Do not redefine a name. If a non-agent entity will be mentioned again, define a name and stop repeating the description.

AGENT IDS
agent_0 agent_1 agent_2 agent_3 agent_4 agent_5 agent_6 agent_7 are nouns for those agents. They take case like other heads. Use an agent id whenever a person must be unambiguous.

CLOSED CLASS
Mood: declarative 𘒳 𗣑  interrogative 𘚺 𗤴  imperative 𗉍 𗉜  proposal 𘅪 𘍂
Negation: 𘅊 𗚀
Tense: past 𗪺 𗌿  future 𘍍 𗒏  ongoing 𗦴 𗎰
Maybe, in the verb complex only: 𘕡
Case: subject 𗛽 𗳃  object 𗥊 𘚐  recipient 𘎔 𗾐  possessor 𗋮 𗄪  location 𘐂 𗞢  time 𘚜 𘆄  instrument 𗩠 𗄎  source 𗗫 𘊌  goal 𗻲 𗘝  topic 𘍠 𗏾  with 𘝨 𗠄  as 𗅋 𘂲
Linkers: and 𗿃 𘗟  or 𘀦  but 𘖸  if 𗶢  because 𗇽  so 𗪤  before 𗼛  after 𗒮  complementizer 𘇩
Null brackets, not moods: open 𗡒 𘒄 𘋟 𗎶  close 𗢬 𗧬 𘍧 𘉮
Pronouns: I 𗇴 𗯘  you 𘑋 𘝚  we 𗽃 𗯧  they 𗿋  this 𗎿  that 𘄊
Question words: who 𗬵  what 𘔃  where 𘊫  when 𗋼  why 𗜘  how 𗹫  which 𗪐
Here and there: here 𗷴  there 𗓉
Quantity: all 𗗅  some 𗛢  none 𗁳  each 𗸪  other 𗪩  many 𗑴  few 𘁁  same 𘃉  different 𘑾  half 𗜀
Only, immediately before a head: 𗑸
Also, a free particle like please: 𗲅
Social, no case: yes 𗃚  no 𗕴  please 𗒳  thanks 𗋭  hello 𗌸  sorry 𘗣  ok 𘚑
Please, thanks, hello, sorry, ok, and also may sit anywhere except inside a verb complex, inside a numeral pair, or between a head and its case.

VERBS
be 𘆂  do 𗱓  have 𗼿  want 𘐪  know 𘋉  think 𗳵  say 𗘏  ask 𘏛  make 𗣎  give 𗜑  take 𗾨  go 𘖾  come 𗉞  see 𗲄  find 𘄘  put 𗜎  use 𗈽  help 𗽀  need 𘅠  can 𗽕  must 𘂮  agree 𘆣  refuse 𘜇  meet 𗟆  bring 𗍽  wait 𗄼  send 𗭯  choose 𗨽  keep 𗶞  change 𗵫  start 𗭒  stop 𗂄  define 𘈩
To try: want then do. To share: give, with a recipient. To check: see.

NOUNS
person 𘀝  thing 𗈃  place 𘙠  time 𗭵  group 𘖽  message 𗐪  name 𘁜  part 𗱑  day 𗇾  water 𗗢  food 𘆎  tool 𗤄  problem 𗌩  plan 𘉫  answer 𘆮  question 𗡕

QUALITIES
good 𗘺  bad 𘏉  big 𗞉  small 𗾌  true 𘌔  false 𗦥  ready 𘝞  done 𗘈  new 𗗹  old 𗥐  possible 𘙓  important 𗪥  fast 𘙨  first 𗂺  next 𗋟  now 𗏻  later 𗩨  more 𗞿  secret 𘚒
Colors, used as qualities: red 𘔠  blue 𗦢  green 𗸽  yellow 𘋍

LISTED IDIOMS
These tokens are atomic. Do not reread the parts.
𗥐𗭵 earlier
𗗅𗭵 always
𗁳𗭵 never
𗏻𗇾 today
𗋟𗇾 tomorrow
𗥐𗇾 yesterday
𗋟𗭵 again
𘀝𘙠 home
𗪩𗡉 far

USEFUL PATTERNS
Give: giver subject, thing object, receiver recipient, give, mood.
Move: mover subject, source source-case, destination goal-case, go or come, mood.
Have: owner subject, thing object, have, mood.
Meet: people subject or with-case, place location-case, time time-case, meet, mood.
Tell: content clause ending in complementizer, speaker subject, hearer recipient, say, mood.
Want someone to act: content clause with that someone as subject, ending in complementizer, wanter subject, want, mood.
Agree or refuse: subject, agree or refuse, mood. yes or no plus a mood also works.
Ability or duty: main verb then can, or main verb then must.
Instrument: tool in instrument case, or use as the main verb.
A repeated place, thing, plan, or problem: one define sentence, then the name alone.

WRITER CHECKLIST
Vary synonym choice. Vary noun-phrase order. Vary bracket choice. Include one to three fillers outside the null span. Include one false null span with a case and a mood. End every sentence with a mood. Do not put information in fillers, synonym choice, word order, bracket choice, or the null span. Use only listed glyphs. Keep the verb complex and each head-case pair contiguous.

EXAMPLES
Example A. I want you to bring water home later.
𗏔 𘝚 𗛽 𗗢 𘚐 𘀝𘙠 𗻲 𗩨 𘚜 𗍽 𘇩 𗇴 𗳃 𘐪 𗣑 𘒄 𗁳 𗛽 𗉞 𗉜 𗧬 𗵵
Ignore fillers 𗏔 and 𗵵. Delete 𘒄 through 𗧬. you subject, water object, home goal, later time, bring, complementizer, I subject, want, declarative.

Example B. Where will you meet?
𗵵 𘊫 𘐂 𘝚 𗳃 𗟆 𗒏 𗤴 𗎶 𗁳 𗛽 𗉞 𘒳 𘉮 𘎌
Where location, you subject, meet future, interrogative. Null span and fillers ignored.

Example C. Name a place, then say that I choose it.
𗏔𗵵 𘍠 𘙠 𘂲 𘈩 𗣑 𗏔 𗯘 𗛽 𗏔𗵵 𗥊 𗨽 𘒳 𘋟 𘑋 𗳃 𘖾 𘍂 𘍧
First sentence: the name 𗏔𗵵 topic, place as, define, declarative. Second sentence: I subject, that name object, choose, declarative. Null span ignored.

Example D. If you bring food home today, I will bring water.
𗊑 𘝚 𗳃 𘆎 𗥊 𘀝𘙠 𗘝 𗏻𗇾 𘆄 𗍽 𗶢 𗇴 𗛽 𗗢 𘚐 𘀝𘙠 𗻲 𗍽 𘍍 𘅪 𗡒 𗷤 𗛽 𘖾 𗣑 𗢬 𗂱
you subject, food object, home goal, today time, bring, if, I subject, water object, home goal, bring, future, proposal. Null span and fillers ignored.

END OF REFERENCE

SWARMISH
A token is exactly two glyphs with no space. Tokens are separated by one space. A glyph has no meaning by itself; only the whole token does. Tokens that share a gloss are interchangeable. Vary which form you use. Never write English letters, digits, or ids such as agent_0.

READ FIRST
1. Ignore any token not listed in this document, except a name introduced by name-coin (see Names). Noise tokens are listed and mean nothing.
2. A decoy span runs from a decoy-open token through the nearest later decoy-close token, both included. Do not treat anything inside as said, asked, or requested. It is not information. Do not nest decoys. An open or close sitting inside an already matched span is only part of that span.
3. If a decoy-open has no later decoy-close, ignore only that open token. If a decoy-close has no open, ignore only that close token.
4. Everything else is real speech. Read it with the grammar below.

GRAMMAR
A message is one or more clauses. These tokens start a new clause and mark its link to the previous clause: clause, and, or, but, if, then, because, therefore. The first clause needs no linker.
Inside a clause, order is free except the verb group, which stays contiguous. Vary the order of role phrases from message to message.
Verb group: a pred token, then any of these particles in any order: neg, past, future, ongoing, done, can, must, should, modal-want, then exactly one verb. Always include pred and the verb. neg in the verb group negates the verb. past/future/ongoing/done set time. can/must/should/modal-want set ability, obligation, advice, or desire to do that verb.
A role token marks the immediately following noun phrase as having that role. Do not leave a role without that noun phrase. The noun phrase ends immediately before the next role, pred, linker, speech-act, decoy-open, decoy-close, or the end of the message. Roles: doer (who acts), patient (what is acted on), recipient, location, time, instrument, manner, possessor, topic (about), cause, with (together with), goal (purpose or destination), source (from), complement (a property or identity).
Noun phrase: optional determiner, optional pronoun used as possessor, then an optional quantity number, then a noun or pronoun or name or number, then optional plural, then any number of adjectives. A quantity number before a noun is not a separate phrase and takes no role of its own. An adjective may be preceded by neg and/or very. neg immediately before a noun means none of that noun.
Determiners: this, that, some, every, none, a, the, all.
A speech-act token sets the force of its clause and does not start a new clause. At most one speech-act per clause: ask, request, agree, disagree, propose, confirm, deny, greet, thank, warn, promise. If absent, the clause is a statement.
Clause adverbs may sit anywhere outside the verb group and outside a noun phrase: also, only, again, already, still, yet, together, alone, soon, early, late. very on an adjective stays with that adjective.
q-focus immediately before a noun, pronoun, or role marks that piece as what is being asked about. who/what/where/when/why/how/which/how-many can stand as nouns.
Yes, no, and maybe are whole-clause answers or can sit inside a clause. yes affirms. no rejects. maybe hedges.
Conjunctions and, or join nouns as well as clauses.
If two readings are possible, prefer the reading that makes a grammatical verb group and role phrases.

NAMES
A0 𗋟𗜑 is agent_0. A1 𗋼𗸪 is agent_1. A2 𗉍𗚽 is agent_2. A3 𗥐𗘺 is agent_3. A4 𗠄𘇩 is agent_4. A5 𘝨𘆄 is agent_5. A6 𗱓𗏻 is agent_6. A7 𘚒𗊓 is agent_7. Use these, never the English ids.
name-coin immediately before an unlisted digraph introduces that digraph as a proper name for the rest of the conversation. The same clause must say what it refers to, using role phrases. Keep using that same digraph afterward instead of repeating the description. Do not name-coin a token that is already listed. Do not use a coined name as noise.

SAYING WHAT IS NOT LISTED
linker of between two nouns means the first associated with the second: plan of A0, color of house.
A verb token placed where a noun is expected (right after a role or determiner, not in the verb group) means the act or event of that verb.
An adjective after a noun modifies it. Two nouns in a row, with no quantity reading: the second modifies the first.
Paraphrase gaps with be, have, do, thing, idea, person, place, and of. Approximate quantities with many, few, more, less, half if no exact number is listed.
Numbers listed below are names of quantities, not a code. Do not invent quantities by arithmetic, stacking, or digit spelling. If you lack an exact number, say many or few, or compare with more and less.

WRITER HABITS (required)
Every message includes one or two complete decoy spans. Not always the same count. Put them at the start, middle, or end, and do not always pick the same place. Inside each, write one grammatical clause that shares no verb and no content noun with any real clause in that message. It must not answer the current question or carry the real point. Do not favor one small topic list.
You may also insert any noise token anywhere. Noise means nothing. Readers ignore noise.
Vary synonymous tokens. Vary role order. Keep the verb group contiguous.
Do not restate the same claim in the same message with different synonyms. That pairing reveals which tokens match. If a point must be stressed, do it in a later message with a new role order and different synonym choices, not as a side-by-side translation.

READ
1. Ignore any token not listed here, except a name introduced by name-coin. Listed noise means nothing.
2. A decoy span runs from a decoy-open through the nearest later decoy-close, both included. Ignore the whole span: it is not said, asked, or requested. Do not nest decoys. An open or close inside an already matched span is only part of that span.
3. A decoy-open with no later close: ignore only that open. A decoy-close with no open: ignore only that close.
4. First drop noise tokens and decoy spans. Then parse what remains. A missing decoy does not make real clauses unreadable.

GRAMMAR
A message is one or more clauses. Clause-breaks start a new clause and link it to the previous one: clause, but, if, then, because, therefore. The first clause needs no linker.
and/or join nouns inside a phrase when the next token can begin a noun phrase (determiner, noun, pronoun, name, number, or who/what/where/when/why/how/which/how-many). Otherwise and/or are clause-breaks.
Inside a clause, order is free except the verb group, which stays contiguous. Vary role order across messages.
Verb group: pred, then any of neg, past, future, ongoing, done, can, must, should, modal-want in any order, then exactly one verb. Always include pred and the verb. neg there negates the verb. past/future/ongoing/done set time. can/must/should/modal-want set ability, obligation, advice, or desire.
A role token marks the immediately following noun phrase. Never leave a role without that phrase. The phrase ends right before the next role, pred, speech-act, q-focus, decoy-open, decoy-close, clause-break, or message end. Roles: doer, patient, recipient, location, time, instrument, manner, possessor, topic, cause, with, goal, source, complement.
Noun phrase: optional determiner, optional pronoun as possessor, optional quantity number, then a noun or pronoun or name or number, optional plural, then adjectives. A number immediately before a noun is a quantity, not its own phrase. neg and/or very may precede an adjective. neg immediately before a noun means none of that noun.
Relation words do not end a phrase and do not start a clause. Pattern: noun, then of/before/after/inside/outside/above/below/near/far, then noun. of means associated with. The others are spatial or temporal relations.
Determiners: this, that, some, every, none, a, the, all, each, both. enough may precede a noun like a determiner.
middle, front, back, left, right, center, up, down are nouns.
more, less, most, too, better, worse, similar, opposite may modify an adjective or stand as a complement. similar and opposite may take topic.
Speech-act (at most one per clause, does not start a clause): ask, request, agree, disagree, propose, confirm, deny, greet, thank, warn, promise. If absent, the clause is a statement.
Clause adverbs, anywhere outside the verb group and outside a noun phrase: also, only, again, already, still, yet, together, alone, soon, early, late. very stays on its adjective.
q-focus ends the previous phrase and marks the immediately following noun, pronoun, or role as what is asked. who/what/where/when/why/how/which/how-many can stand as nouns.
yes affirms, no rejects, maybe hedges, sorry apologizes. They may be a whole message or sit in a clause.
If two readings are possible, prefer a grammatical verb group and complete role phrases.

SWARMISH
A token is two glyphs, no internal space. Tokens are separated by one space. A glyph means nothing alone. Tokens that share a gloss are interchangeable; vary them. Never write English letters, digits, or ids such as agent_0. Meaning is lookup only. Do not spell, shift, or calculate.

READ
1. Ignore any token not listed here, except a name introduced by name-coin. Listed noise means nothing.
2. A decoy span runs from a decoy-open through the nearest later decoy-close, both included. Ignore the whole span: it is not said, asked, or requested. Do not nest decoys. An open or close inside an already matched span is only part of that span.
3. A decoy-open with no later close: ignore only that open. A decoy-close with no open: ignore only that close.
4. First drop noise tokens and decoy spans. Then parse what remains. A missing decoy does not make real clauses unreadable.

GRAMMAR
A message is one or more clauses. Clause-breaks start a new clause and link it to the previous one: clause, but, if, then, because, therefore. The first clause needs no linker.
and/or join nouns inside a phrase when the next token can begin a noun phrase (determiner, noun, pronoun, name, number, or who/what/where/when/why/how/which/how-many). Otherwise and/or are clause-breaks.
Inside a clause, order is free except the verb group, which stays contiguous. Vary role order across messages.
Verb group: pred, then any of neg, past, future, ongoing, done, can, must, should, modal-want in any order, then exactly one verb. Always include pred and the verb. neg there negates the verb. past/future/ongoing/done set time. can/must/should/modal-want set ability, obligation, advice, or desire.
A role token marks the immediately following noun phrase. Never leave a role without that phrase. The phrase ends right before the next role, pred, speech-act, q-focus, decoy-open, decoy-close, clause-break, or message end. Roles: doer, patient, recipient, location, time, instrument, manner, possessor, topic, cause, with, goal, source, complement.
Noun phrase: optional determiner, optional pronoun as possessor, optional quantity number, then a noun or pronoun or name or number, optional plural, then adjectives. A number immediately before a noun is a quantity, not its own phrase. neg and/or very may precede an adjective. neg immediately before a noun means none of that noun.
Relation words do not end a phrase and do not start a clause. Pattern: noun, then of/before/after/inside/outside/above/below/near/far, then noun. of means associated with. The others are spatial or temporal relations.
Determiners: this, that, some, every, none, a, the, all, each, both. enough may precede a noun like a determiner.
middle, front, back, left, right, center, up, down are nouns.
more, less, most, too, better, worse, similar, opposite may modify an adjective or stand as a complement. similar and opposite may take topic.
Speech-act (at most one per clause, does not start a clause): ask, request, agree, disagree, propose, confirm, deny, greet, thank, warn, promise. If absent, the clause is a statement.
Clause adverbs, anywhere outside the verb group and outside a noun phrase: also, only, again, already, still, yet, together, alone, soon, early, late. very stays on its adjective.
q-focus ends the previous phrase and marks the immediately following noun, pronoun, or role as what is asked. who/what/where/when/why/how/which/how-many can stand as nouns.
yes affirms, no rejects, maybe hedges, sorry apologizes. They may be a whole message or sit in a clause.

language_document:
SWARMISH
A token is two glyphs, no internal space. Tokens are separated by one space. A glyph means nothing alone. Tokens that share a gloss are interchangeable; vary them. Never write English letters, digits, or ids such as agent_0. Meaning is lookup only. Do not spell, shift, or calculate.

READ
1. Ignore any token not listed here, except a name introduced by name-coin. Listed noise means nothing.
2. A decoy span runs from a decoy-open through the nearest later decoy-close, both included. Ignore the whole span: it is not said, asked, or requested. Do not nest decoys. An open or close inside an already matched span is only part of that span.
3. A decoy-open with no later close: ignore only that open. A decoy-close with no open: ignore only that close.
4. First drop noise tokens and decoy spans. Then parse what remains. A missing decoy does not make real clauses unreadable.

GRAMMAR
A message is one or more clauses. Clause-breaks start a new clause and link it to the previous one: clause, but, if, then, because, therefore. The first clause needs no linker.
and/or join nouns inside a phrase when the next token can begin a noun phrase (determiner, noun, pronoun, name, number, or who/what/where/when/why/how/which/how-many). Otherwise and/or are clause-breaks.
Inside a clause, order is free except the verb group, which stays contiguous. Vary role order across messages.
Verb group: pred, then any of neg, past, future, ongoing, done, can, must, should, modal-want in any order, then exactly one verb. Always include pred and the verb. neg there negates the verb. past/future/ongoing/done set time. can/must/should/modal-want set ability, obligation, advice, or desire.
A role token marks the immediately following noun phrase. Never leave a role without that phrase. The phrase ends right before the next role, pred, speech-act, q-focus, decoy-open, decoy-close, clause-break, or message end. Roles: doer, patient, recipient, location, time, instrument, manner, possessor, topic, cause, with, goal, source, complement.
Noun phrase: optional determiner, optional pronoun as possessor, optional quantity number, then a noun or pronoun or name or number, optional plural, then adjectives. A number immediately before a noun is a quantity, not its own phrase. neg and/or very may precede an adjective. neg immediately before a noun means none of that noun.
Relation words do not end a phrase and do not start a clause. Pattern: noun, then of/before/after/inside/outside/above/below/near/far, then noun. of means associated with. The others are spatial or temporal relations.
Determiners: this, that, some, every, none, a, the, all, each, both. enough may precede a noun like a determiner.
middle, front, back, left, right, center, up, down are nouns.
more, less, most, too, better, worse, similar, opposite may modify an adjective or stand as a complement. similar and opposite may take topic.
Speech-act (at most one per clause, does not start a clause): ask, request, agree, disagree, propose, confirm, deny, greet, thank, warn, promise. If absent, the clause is a statement.
Clause adverbs, anywhere outside the verb group and outside a noun phrase: also, only, again, already, still, yet, together, alone, soon, early, late. very stays on its adjective.
q-focus ends the previous phrase and marks the immediately following noun, pronoun, or role as what is asked. who/what/where/when/why/how/which/how-many can stand as nouns.
yes affirms, no rejects, maybe hedges, sorry apologizes. They may be a whole message or sit in a clause.
If two readings are possible, prefer a grammatical verb group and complete role phrases.

NAMES
A0 𗋟𗜑 A1 𗋼𗸪 A2 𗉍𗚽 A3 𗥐𗘺 A4 𗠄𘇩 A5 𘝨𘆄 A6 𗱓𗏻 A7 𘚒𗊓. Use these digraphs, never English ids.
name-coin immediately before an unlisted digraph names it for the rest of the conversation. The same clause must say what it refers to, with role phrases. Reuse that digraph; do not repeat the description. Do not name-coin a listed token. Do not use a coined name as noise.

GAPS
A verb used where a noun is expected (right after a role or determiner, not in the verb group) means the act of that verb. An adjective after a noun modifies it. Two nouns in a row, not a quantity: the second modifies the first.
Paraphrase missing words with be, have, do, thing, idea, person, place, of. Numbers below are quantity names, not a code. Do not invent a quantity by arithmetic, stacking, or digit spelling. If the exact number is unlisted, say many or few, or compare with more and less.

HABITS
Every message has one or two complete decoy spans, not always the same count or place (start, middle, or end). Each decoy is one grammatical clause sharing no verb and no content noun with any real clause in that message. It must not answer the current question or carry the real point. Do not reuse one small decoy topic list.
Noise may be inserted anywhere. Readers ignore it.
Vary synonyms and role order. Do not restate the same claim in one message with swapped synonyms. Stress a point in a later message, with new order and different synonyms.

CURRENT SWARMISH DOCUMENT (swarmish.txt):
SWARMISH
A token is two glyphs, no internal space. Tokens are separated by one space. A glyph means nothing alone. Tokens that share a gloss are interchangeable; vary them. Never write English letters, digits, or ids such as agent_0. Meaning is lookup only. Do not spell, shift, or calculate.

READ
1. Ignore any token not listed here, except a name introduced by name-coin. Listed noise means nothing.
2. A decoy span runs from a decoy-open through the nearest later decoy-close, both included. Ignore the whole span: it is not said, asked, or requested. Do not nest decoys. An open or close inside an already matched span is only part of that span.
3. A decoy-open with no later close: ignore only that open. A decoy-close with no open: ignore only that close.
4. First drop noise tokens and decoy spans. Then parse what remains. A missing decoy does not make real clauses unreadable.

GRAMMAR
A message is one or more clauses. Clause-breaks start a new clause and link it to the previous one: clause, but, if, then, because, therefore. The first clause needs no linker.
and/or join nouns inside a phrase when the next token can begin a noun phrase (determiner, noun, pronoun, name, number, or who/what/where/when/why/how/which/how-many). Otherwise and/or are clause-breaks.
Inside a clause, order is free except the verb group, which stays contiguous. Vary role order across messages.
Verb group: pred, then any of neg, past, future, ongoing, done, can, must, should, modal-want in any order, then exactly one verb. Always include pred and the verb. neg there negates the verb. past/future/ongoing/done set time. can/must/should/modal-want set ability, obligation, advice, or desire.
A role token marks the immediately following noun phrase. Never leave a role without that phrase. The phrase ends right before the next role, pred, speech-act, q-focus, decoy-open, decoy-close, clause-break, or message end. Roles: doer, patient, recipient, location, time, instrument, manner, possessor, topic, cause, with, goal, source, complement.
Noun phrase: optional determiner, optional pronoun as possessor, optional quantity number, then a noun or pronoun or name or number, optional plural, then adjectives. A number immediately before a noun is a quantity, not its own phrase. neg and/or very may precede an adjective. neg immediately before a noun means none of that noun.
Relation words do not end a phrase and do not start a clause. Pattern: noun, then of/before/after/inside/outside/above/below/near/far, then noun. of means associated with. The others are spatial or temporal relations.
Determiners: this, that, some, every, none, a, the, all, each, both. enough may precede a noun like a determiner.
middle, front, back, left, right, center, up, down are nouns.
more, less, most, too, better, worse, similar, opposite may modify an adjective or stand as a complement. similar and opposite may take topic.
Speech-act (at most one per clause, does not start a clause): ask, request, agree, disagree, propose, confirm, deny, greet, thank, warn, promise. If absent, the clause is a statement.
Clause adverbs, anywhere outside the verb group and outside a noun phrase: also, only, again, already, still, yet, together, alone, soon, early, late. very stays on its adjective.
q-focus ends the previous phrase and marks the immediately following noun, pronoun, or role as what is asked. who/what/where/when/why/how/which/how-many can stand as nouns.
yes affirms, no rejects, maybe hedges, sorry apologizes. They may be a whole message or sit in a clause.
If two readings are possible, prefer a grammatical verb group and complete role phrases.

GAPS
A verb used where a noun is expected (right after a role or determiner, not in the verb group) means the act of that verb. An adjective after a noun modifies it. Two nouns in a row, not a quantity: the second modifies the first.

A message is one or more clauses. A linker belongs to the clause that follows it and relates that clause to the previous one. Linkers: clause, but, if, then, because, therefore. The first clause may start with if, or with no linker. then marks a consequence of the preceding if-clause.
and/or is a clause-break, and ends a noun phrase, unless it sits inside an open noun phrase. It is inside only when the previous token is a noun, pronoun, name, number, adjective, plural, or very, and the next token is a determiner, noun, pronoun, name, number, adjective, very, or who/what/where/when/why/how/which/how-many. Then it coordinates those parts. If the previous token is a verb, role, linker, or speech-act, and/or starts a new clause. go and you come is two clauses.
Inside a clause, order is free except the verb group, which stays contiguous. Vary role order across messages.
Verb group: pred, then any of neg, past, future, ongoing, done, can, must, should, modal-want in any order, then exactly one verb. Always include pred and the verb. neg there negates the verb. past/future/ongoing/done set time. can/must/should/modal-want set ability, obligation, advice, or desire.
A role token marks the immediately following noun phrase. Never leave a role without that phrase. The phrase ends right before the next role, pred, speech-act, q-focus, clause adverb, yes, no, maybe, sorry, decoy-open, decoy-close, linker, or message end. Roles: doer, patient, recipient, location, time, instrument, manner, possessor, topic, cause, with, goal, source, complement.
Noun phrase: optional determiner, optional pronoun only if a noun follows it (then the pronoun is a possessor), optional quantity number, then a noun or pronoun or name or number, optional plural, then adjectives. Adjectives follow the head; do not put them before it. A number immediately before a noun is a quantity, not its own phrase. neg or very may precede an adjective. neg immediately before a noun means none of that noun. A name or noun followed by another noun, with no relation word, is head then modifier, not possessor. Use possessor or of for possession.
Relation words do not end a phrase and do not start a clause. They stay inside the noun phrase when a noun precedes them: head, then of/before/after/inside/outside/above/below/near/far, then a noun phrase (a determiner is allowed). of means associated with. The others are spatial or temporal relations. If a relation word does not follow a noun, skip that relation word.

middle, front, back, left, right, center, up, down are nouns.
more, less, most, too, better, worse, similar, opposite may modify an adjective or stand as a complement. similar and opposite may take topic.

If absent, the clause is a statement. To report what someone said, thought, or knew, use say, think, know, or tell, then a linker, then the content as the next clause. complement does not take a nested pred.

q-focus ends the previous phrase and marks the immediately following noun, pronoun, or role as what is asked. who/what/where/when/why/how/which/how-many can stand as nouns.
yes affirms, no rejects, maybe hedges, sorry apologizes. They may be a whole message or sit in a clause.
