language_document:
SWARMISH REFERENCE
Read this whole file before writing. Messages may contain only Swarmish glyphs and spaces. Never write Latin letters, digits, punctuation, or labels such as agent_0. Do not spell English glyph by glyph. Do not use binary, place value as a code, or any calculation. A glyph means nothing alone. Only a listed two-glyph pair, or a coined name, has a meaning. Look pairs up. Do not compute.

WORD SHAPE
Separate words with single spaces. Every word is exactly two glyphs. A longer or shorter token is a mistake: ignore that token and keep reading. Do not invent listed words. If a meaning is missing, circumlocute, or coin a name and define it.
A coined name is 𘆄 plus one other glyph. No listed word begins with 𘆄. Until defined, 𘆄 plus a glyph has no known meaning: ask, do not guess.

NOISE
These words mean nothing. Delete every noise word before any other reading. They may stand anywhere.
Noise: 𗟎𗥐 𗪩𘙓 𗇽𗕴 𘉮𗭒 𗑴𘚜 𘋟𗲅 𗗹𘏉 𘆮𗦴 𗌸𗼛 𗗅𗪤 𘍄𘛺 𘗣𗒮
Every message uses at least two noise words. Do not reuse a noise word from your previous message.

DECOY SPANS
After noise is deleted, delete every decoy span: from a decoy-open through the next decoy-close, including both. Do not nest decoys. If an open has no later close, delete only the open. If a close has no earlier open, delete only the close. A message with no decoy is still valid.
A decoy is a grammatical false or irrelevant clause. Never put the only copy of a needed fact in a decoy. Do not repeat another speaker's decoy. A decoy must not differ from a real clause by only one word. Vary whether the decoy is first, medial, or last.

HOW TO READ
Split on spaces. Delete noise. Delete decoy spans. Split the rest into clauses at mood words. The mood word types the clause and is not content. Do not count, shift, or compute.
If a clause begins with a linker, that linker joins it to the previous clause. Linkers are and, or, but, if, therefore, because, purpose, and content. Remove the linker before reading roles. A linker not at the start of a clause is a mistake: ignore it.
Flavor words may stand anywhere and do not take roles: please, thanks, sorry, hello, perhaps. Set them aside.
A verb-marker plus the next word, then an optional evidential, then an optional negation, is the verb group. Evidentials are only certain, inferred, reported, and unsure. Those words stay together. Remove the group. The word after the verb-marker is the verb. An adjective there means be that property.
If already, not-yet, again, can, must, or try stands immediately before the verb-marker, it modifies the predicate. Ignore those words elsewhere unless can, must, or try is itself the verb. If no verb-marker remains, the clause is minor: a discourse word such as yes, no, or acknowledged, plus its mood. A minor clause needs no case-word.
What remains is a sequence of case phrases. A case-word ends a phrase. Words before it are the noun phrase. An address-word ends a vocative, not a role. A topic-word ends a topic, not a role. If words remain with no ending case, address, or topic word, ask for repair. That repair rule does not apply to a minor clause.
Noun phrase: the last word is the head, unless and-np coordinates the word before it and the word after it. A leading focus-word, only-word, or also-word marks the phrase and is not the head. Other preceding words are determiners, adjectives, or a number-name. very, almost, more, less, most, and enough modify the next adjective or number. A plural-word before a head pluralizes it.
A number-name is one number word, or a decade word immediately followed by a unit word, or 100 or 1000 immediately followed by one such name. 𘊫𗍽 𘁁𗶢 is the name twenty-two. 𗤄𘗟 𘊫𗍽 𘁁𗶢 is the name one hundred twenty-two. Copy only that shape. The sequence is the name; do not add, multiply, or invent another base. If unsure, use one listed number word.
Same-case phrases are two or more participants in that role, not a different role. and-np under one case-word is coordination.

CLAUSE MEANING
Phrase order is free. Vary it. Roles come only from case-words. No tense. Default time is now. A time noun plus a time-case sets time. A place noun plus a locative sets place.
A request with no nominative asks you. A proposal with no nominative proposes that we act. Any other clause with no nominative has the speaker as actor.
A yes-no question has statement shape and a question mood. A content question puts the interrogative in the asked role and uses a question mood.
Negation in the verb group negates the predicate. For no X, use the none determiner.
A genitive phrase possesses the noun phrase it touches: the phrase before it, or, if the genitive is first, the phrase after it. Comparison: the adjective is the verb, and the standard takes than.
Be equates nominative with accusative. Be with a locative and no accusative means be at that place.
Give, show, tell, offer: nominative acts, accusative is the theme, dative is the recipient.
Put: nominative puts accusative at a locative. Take or bring: nominative moves accusative from a from-phrase toward a toward-phrase or locative.
Call: nominative calls accusative, and an as-phrase gives the role or name. Choose, want, need, have, lack: nominative toward accusative.
An if-clause is a condition. A therefore-clause is its consequence. Because gives a reason. Purpose gives a purpose. A content linker means this clause is what the previous say, tell, ask, or answer clause said. And, or, and but join clauses as labeled.

NAMES
Define a name in one real clause, never inside a decoy: a define-word, the coined name, the describing noun phrase with no case-word, a verb-marker, a be-verb, and a statement mood. After that, the name means that noun phrase. Do not repeat the describing phrase.
A mention-word immediately before a word talks about that word instead of using it.
Participants: 𗢬𗊑 agent-0; 𘝄𗡒 agent-1; 𗛢𗊓 agent-2; 𗲄𗞢 agent-3; 𘒄𘅌 agent-4; 𗯘𗨥 agent-5; 𗌿𘍍 agent-6; 𘂲𗧬 agent-7.
Use only these pairs for the eight participants.

VARIATION
Glyphs in one glossary entry mean the same thing. Do not use the same pair for that meaning in your next clause when another pair is listed. If only one pair is listed, reuse it. A repeated pair still means what the glossary says. Do not restate one claim with swapped synonyms. After one definition, use the coined name, not the gloss. These habits are lookup choices, not a code.

SWARMISH REFERENCE

Look up whole words. A word is exactly two glyphs. One glyph has no meaning. Do not split a word, spell with glyphs, count positions, shift, or calculate. Meaning is only the gloss written here.

LAW
- Messages are space-separated words. Each word is two glyphs from the lists below. No Latin letters, no digits, no punctuation, and no agent id such as agent_0.
- Each listed pair has one gloss. Pairs are not reused. If a pair is not listed, ignore that word. Do not invent a meaning.
- Words joined by OR are the same word. The left one is not the default. When a word has two forms, do not use the same form you used in your previous message.
- Every message needs at least one real clause, one or two decoy clauses, and at least two noise words. Do not reuse a noise pair from your previous message. Vary role order. Do not reuse one template.
- Do not send two real clauses that mean the same thing. A decoy is not a paraphrase of the real clause.
- Refer to yourself with an I word. Use an agent-name only for someone else.
- If a referent will be repeated, bind a shell and keep using the shell.
- A missing decoy, a missing noise word, or an unknown pair does not make the message unreadable. Writers still include them.

1 PARSE
Split on spaces. Drop empty pieces. Delete every noise word before any other step. Noise may stand anywhere, including between a role and its body.
Then read left to right. A clause starts at the first remaining word, or after an END.
If the first word of a clause is DECOY, ignore that clause through its END. It is not a claim. A message may have one or two decoys. Put the decoy first in some messages and after a real clause in others. Fill a decoy with a side remark, greeting, or minor fact. Never put the operative claim only in a decoy.
If no decoy is present, read every clause as real. If DECOY is not the first word of its clause, ignore that one word only.
END ends a clause. If the message has no final END, the end of the message still ends the clause.
QUOTE opens a quote and QUOTE-CLOSE closes it. Do not put END, DECOY, or another QUOTE inside a quote. If END appears while a quote is open, close the quote and the clause there. Text after that END is a new clause.
and or or, when it is the first word of a clause, joins that clause to the previous real clause and is not part of a body. and adds. or offers an alternative.

2 CLAUSE
These may stand in any order among role phrases: TYPE, MOOD, MODAL, NEG, CONTRAST.
Missing TYPE means statement. Missing MOOD means certain. Use at most one TYPE, one MOOD, and one MODAL. NEG denies the whole clause. CONTRAST marks a contrast with the previous real clause.
A real clause needs one pred role. If several pred roles appear, the first is the predicate. Later pred roles, and the bodies after them, are ignored.
A role phrase is a role word plus one body. Role phrases stand in any order. Two phrases with the same role are two bodies, not one compound.
A role word with no body is ignored.

3 BODY
A body is one of these:
- QUOTE, then inner words, then QUOTE-CLOSE. Inner words may be clause-level words and role phrases. They may not be DECOY or QUOTE. The quote is the whole body of the role that opened it.
- An amount-name, alone or before a head. One number word names that amount. twenty, thirty, forty, fifty, or sixty immediately followed by one through nine is the ordinary two-word name, such as twenty-three. That is a name, not a sum and not a column code. Do not add, multiply, or assign column values. The amount-name quantifies a following noun when one is present.
- Otherwise: optional MODs, then one or more content words. The last content word is the head. Earlier content words narrow it. private then thing means a thing that is private. MOD applies to that head. MOD not denies only the next content word.
Order inside a non-quote body: amount-name if any, then MODs if any, then content words, last is head.
A body ends at the next role word, clause-level word, linker, or END, once an open quote has taken QUOTE-CLOSE.
Content words are the content list, the number list, the agent-name list, the pronoun list, and shells.

4 NAMES
Pronouns: I, you, we, they, it, someone, everyone, other, this, that.
you is the addressee. If the addressee is unclear, put that teammate's agent-name in topic or recip.
it is the thing or claim just mentioned. this is the current one. that is an earlier one.
Agent-names, in chat-label order from agent_0 through agent_7, are in the name list. The chat label outside the message is not a Swarmish word.
Shells start unbound. A real clause binds a shell only in this frame: pred is name, obj is an unbound shell, topic is the description. After that, the shell means that description for the rest of the conversation. Do not bind one shell twice. Do not put the description in the obj.

5 HOW TO SAY THINGS
State with statement, or with no TYPE. Ask with ask. A yes-no ask has no question word. A content ask puts who, what, where, when, why, how, which, or howmany in the role being asked.
Reply with reply. The pred is yes, no, unknown, or maybe.
Request with request and mood polite. Propose with propose.
Agree: pred agree, obj it. Reject: pred reject, or NEG on the denied clause. Accept: pred accept.
Possession: owner role, or pred have.
Place: place role. Source: source role. Motion: pred move, come, or go. Company or instrument: with role.
Time: time role. before and after are content words in that body.
Cause: cause role. Condition: cond role. Its body is usually a quote.
A quoted claim is a quote in the obj of say, tell, or ask.
Comparison: MOD more or less on the quality, than role for the standard.
Degree: MOD very. Word denial: MOD not directly before the denied word. Clause denial: NEG.
If a concept is missing, paraphrase with thing, person, place, time, way, reason, result, problem, task, tool, goal, group, part, or whole, then ask whether the paraphrase is correct.
Once a shell is bound, do not repeat the long description.
Omit a role only when the previous real clause made it obvious.

SWARMISH REFERENCE

Look up whole words. A word is exactly two glyphs. One glyph has no meaning, even if two words share a glyph. Do not split a word, spell with glyphs, count positions, shift, or calculate. Meaning is only the gloss written here.

LAW
- Messages are space-separated words. Each word is two glyphs from the lists below. No Latin letters, no digits, no punctuation, and no agent id such as agent_0.
- Each listed pair has one gloss. Pairs are not reused. If a pair is not listed, ignore that word. Do not invent a meaning.
- Words joined by OR are the same word. Forms of one word do not share a glyph. The left form is not the default. If your previous message used one form, use a different form this time. On a first message, any form is allowed.
- Every message needs at least one real clause, one or two decoy clauses, and at least two noise words. Do not reuse a noise pair from your previous message. Vary role order. Do not reuse one template.
- Do not send two real clauses that mean the same thing. A decoy is not a paraphrase of the real clause. Do not repeat another agent's claim with the synonyms swapped.
- Refer to yourself with an I word. Use an agent-name only for someone else.
- If a referent will be repeated, bind a shell and keep using the shell. Do not repeat the long description.
- A missing decoy, a missing noise word, or an unknown pair does not make the message unreadable. Writers still include them.

1 PARSE
Split on spaces. Drop empty pieces. Delete every noise word before any other step. Noise may stand anywhere, including between a role and its body.
Then read left to right. A clause starts at the first remaining word, or after an END.
If the first word of a clause is DECOY, ignore that clause through its END. It is not a claim. A message may have one or two decoys. Put the decoy first in some messages and after a real clause in others. Fill a decoy with a side remark, greeting, or minor fact. Never put the operative claim only in a decoy.
If no decoy is present, read every clause as real. If DECOY is not the first word of its clause, ignore that one word only.
END ends a clause. If the message has no final END, the end of the message still ends the clause.
QUOTE opens a quote and QUOTE-CLOSE closes it. Do not put END, DECOY, or another QUOTE inside a quote. If END appears while a quote is open, close the quote and the clause there. Text after that END is a new clause.
A linker joins clauses only when it is the first word of a clause. and adds the new clause to the previous real clause. or offers an alternative. The linker itself is not part of a body. Anywhere else, a linker is ignored and does not join words.

2 CLAUSE
These may stand in any order among role phrases: TYPE, MOOD, MODAL, NEG, CONTRAST.
Missing TYPE means statement. Missing MOOD means certain. Use at most one TYPE, one MOOD, and one MODAL outside quotes. NEG denies the whole clause. CONTRAST marks a contrast with the previous real clause.
Words inside a quote belong only to the quote. The outer clause does not see them. They are not the outer predicate, and they do not end the outer body.
A real clause needs one pred role outside quotes. The first pred outside quotes is the predicate. A later pred outside quotes, and the body after it, is ignored.
A role phrase is a role word plus one body. Role phrases stand in any order. Two phrases with the same role are two bodies of that role, not one compound. Repeat the role word to name two things.
A role word with no body is ignored.

3 BODY
A body is one of these:
- QUOTE, then inner words, then QUOTE-CLOSE. Inner words may be clause-level words and role phrases. They may not be DECOY, END, or QUOTE. The quote is the whole body of the role that opened it. The body does not extend past QUOTE-CLOSE.
- An amount-name, alone or before a head. One number word names that amount. A listed two-word amount-name is one name, not a sum and not a column code. Do not add, multiply, or assign column values. The amount-name quantifies a following noun when one is present.
- Otherwise: optional MODs, then one or more content words. The last content word is the head. Earlier content words narrow it. private then thing means a thing that is private. MOD applies to that head. MOD not denies only the next content word.
Order inside a non-quote body: amount-name if any, then MODs if any, then content words, last is head.
A non-quote body ends at the next role word, clause-level word, linker, or END.
Content words are the content list, the number list, the agent-name list, the pronoun list, and shells.

4 NAMES
Pronouns: I, you, we, they, it, someone, everyone, other, this, that.
you is the addressee. If the addressee is unclear, put that teammate's agent-name in topic or recip.
it is the thing or claim just mentioned. this is the current one. that is an earlier one.
Agent-names, in chat-label order from agent_0 through agent_7, are in the name list. The chat label outside the message is not a Swarmish word.
Shells start unbound. A real clause binds a shell only in this frame: pred is name, obj is an unbound shell, topic is the description. After that, the shell means that description for the rest of the conversation. Do not bind one shell twice. Do not put the description in the obj. A decoy cannot bind a shell.

5 HOW TO SAY THINGS
State with statement, or with no TYPE. Ask with ask. A yes-no ask has no question word. A content ask puts who, what, where, when, why, how, which, or howmany in the role being asked.
Reply with reply. The pred is yes, no, unknown, or maybe.
Request with request and mood polite. Propose with propose.
Agree: pred agree, obj it. Reject: pred reject, or NEG on the denied clause. Accept: pred accept.
Possession: owner role, or pred have.
Place: place role. Source: source role. Motion: pred move, come, or go. Company or instrument: with role.
Time: time role. before and after are content words in that body.
Cause: cause role. Condition: cond role. Its body is usually a quote.
A quoted claim is a quote in the obj of say, tell, or ask.
Comparison: MOD more or less on the quality, than role for the standard.
Degree: MOD very. Word denial: MOD not directly before the denied word. Clause denial: NEG.
Two things in one role: repeat the role word. Do not put and or or between them.
If a concept is missing, paraphrase with thing, person, place, time, way, reason, result, problem, task, tool, goal, group, part, or whole, then ask whether the paraphrase is correct.

Complementizer: the clause ending with the complementizer is the content of the next verb. Noun phrases before the complementizer belong to the content clause. Noun phrases between the complementizer and the next verb belong to that next verb. Content verbs are say, know, think, ask, hear, and want. Put the content clause first.

NOUN PHRASE
A noun phrase is a head followed by one case particle, with nothing between them except a location spatial or a head-joining and or or chain. Clause markers and fillers do not count as between them.
Heads: a content glyph, a compound, a listed idiom, a numeral, a numeral pair, a name, a pronoun, a question word, a quantity glyph, a quality glyph, a spatial glyph used as a head, or an agent id.
Only, quality glyphs, one quantity glyph, one numeral token, or one bound numeral pair may stand before the head and modify it. They may stack. A modifier applies only to the next head, not to a whole and-chain. A numeral pair modifies only when a case does not follow the pair. A quantity or numeral with its own case is a head, not a modifier.
𗞉 immediately before a quality means very. Elsewhere 𗞉 means big.
𗞿 immediately before a quality means more. Elsewhere 𗞿 means more as its own word.
𗾌 immediately before a quality means less. Elsewhere 𗾌 means small.
A possessor is a noun phrase in possessor case immediately before the possessed head. The outer case follows the possessed head. A possessor phrase that is not immediately before a head is a clause-level owner.
Heads joined by and, or by or, with one case particle after the last head, are one phrase and share that role. A head before and or or is not bare. Do not skip it. The shared case belongs to every head in that chain. Modifiers between and and the next head belong to that next head.
A spatial glyph may sit between a head and its case particle. It builds a location on that head. house inside location-case means in the house. That case belongs to the house, not to inside. Do not skip the house. A spatial glyph in any other slot is an ordinary head and needs its own case.

Question words take the case of the role asked. who subject asks who acts. where location asks where.
A listed numeral pair is one numeral, not two bare heads. If a case follows it, it is one head. If it modifies a following head, do not skip it. Any other bare head with no case, and not modifying the next head, is skipped. Do not give the next head's case to a skipped token. A compound has no space. Two adjacent noun tokens are not a compound.

NUMERALS
These tokens are atomic names. They are not digits. Do not add, multiply, or build other values. A numeral before a head modifies that head. See NOUN PHRASE.

A token of exactly two filler glyphs, with no space, is a name. It means nothing until defined. Do not translate its parts.

USEFUL PATTERNS

language_document:
SWARMISH REFERENCE
Only this file defines Swarmish. Read the whole file before writing. Glyphs are meaningless alone except as listed. If two rules seem to conflict, follow HOW TO READ, then NOUN PHRASE, then the tables.

CHARACTERS
A message may contain only spaces, the tokens agent_0 agent_1 agent_2 agent_3 agent_4 agent_5 agent_6 agent_7, and glyphs listed below. No other digits, punctuation, line breaks, or marks. Agent ids are the exception: copy them exactly, underscore and digit included. One message is one line. Split on spaces. Ignore empty tokens. One token is one word. Never glue a particle onto another glyph. Compounds, listed idioms, and names are single tokens of glued glyphs. A listed numeral pair is two tokens. Copy glyphs from the tables. Any other character, including a digit outside those eight agent ids, rejects the whole message. Do not invent a glyph.

HOW TO READ
1. Delete every null span before any other parse. An open bracket is 𗡒 or 𘒄 or 𘋟 or 𗎶. A close bracket is 𗢬 or 𘉮 or 𘍧. From an open through the next close, delete both brackets and everything between them. If an open has no later close, ignore only that open. A close with no earlier open is ignored. Do not nest brackets. A null span is not a claim. Do not believe it or act on it. Where a span sits carries no meaning.
2. Delete every remaining token that is exactly one filler glyph. A missing filler, an extra filler, or a missing null span does not make a message unreadable.
3. When asking what immediately follows a token, skip 𗒳 𗋭 𗌸 𘗣 𘚑 𗲅. Those are clause markers, not heads and not verbs. Do not delete them.
4. If two neighboring tokens are a listed numeral pair, bind them as one numeral before any skip rule. A case after the pair makes that numeral a head. A following head, only, or quality makes it a modifier of that head. Do not add the parts. No unlisted pair is a numeral. A single numeral token or quantity glyph before a head modifies that head.
5. Split what remains into sentences at each mood glyph. The mood belongs to the sentence before it. If no mood remains, read the message as one declarative sentence.
6. Inside a sentence, a linker that follows a verb complex ends that clause and joins it to the next. and and or do not do this when they join heads, as in NOUN PHRASE. Any glyph in a linker row is that linker.
7. Look up tokens in the tables. Check listed idioms before compounds. Do not calculate, count positions, or spell with English.
8. Case marks role. Noun-phrase order does not mark role. Vary that order.
9. Skip a token that is not listed, not an idiom, not part of a bound numeral, not a compound, not a name, and not an agent id, unless NOUN PHRASE says it belongs to a larger phrase. Skip a case particle that attaches to nothing. Skip a linker that neither ends a verb complex nor joins heads.

FILLERS
These six glyphs mean nothing alone. A one-glyph token of one of them is deleted before parsing. Every message must contain one, two, or three filler tokens outside every null span. Filler choice and filler count carry no meaning. Write each filler as its own token. Never insert a filler glyph into a compound, idiom, or name. A filler between tokens is deleted, so it does not keep a head from its case.
Fillers: 𗏔 𗵵 𘎌 𗊑 𗂱 𗟎

NULL SPAN
Every message must contain one or two null spans. Inside each, write a false or irrelevant clause of at least two tokens, including one case particle and one mood, so it looks like Swarmish. Do not reuse a noun, verb, idiom, quality, numeral, or name glyph from outside the span. Function glyphs may repeat. Do not paraphrase the real claim. Readers delete every span first. Writers must vary which open and which close they use, and must vary putting the span at the start, in the middle, or at the end. The choice carries no meaning. Do not hide real task content in a span. Do not break a head-case pair, a numeral pair, or a verb complex with a span. A message that lacks a span is still readable. Bracket glyphs are never words. 𗎶 only opens a null span. It does not mean back.

SYNONYMS
Two or more glyphs listed for one meaning are identical. Readers accept any. Writers must vary the choice across a message and a conversation, and must not always pick the leftmost glyph in a row. A row of three is still one meaning; use all three over a conversation. The choice carries no information. Do not tie a synonym to an agent id. Do not restate the same claim with swapped synonyms in one message.

SENTENCE SHAPE
A clause is any number of noun phrases, in any order, then one verb complex, then one mood or one linker. Exception: heads joined by and or or share one case particle after the last head. That chain is one noun phrase.
A mood ends the sentence. A linker does not. It joins this clause to the next clause in the same sentence.
For if, because, so, before, after, and the complementizer: finish the whole first clause, including its noun phrases and its verb, before any noun phrase of the next clause. Do not put the next clause's subject first. An English order such as I want you to bring will be misread.
Several sentences may share one message.
Verb complex, contiguous, immediately before the mood or linker: one or more verb glyphs, or one verb idiom, then an optional negation glyph, then an optional tense glyph, then an optional maybe glyph. Clause markers are invisible to adjacency. They may sit in the complex and are not part of it. They do not break contiguity. Negation, tense, and maybe cover the whole chain. Omitted tense means present or unspecified. Omitted maybe means the claim is plain, not uncertain.
can and must govern the other verb and are not the event. Normal order is verb then can, or verb then must: bring can means can bring; bring must means must bring. If can or must is elsewhere in the chain, it still governs and is not the event. For every other verb row, the last verb is the main verb and each earlier verb modifies it: go want means want to go.
A quality glyph in the verb complex means be that quality. No copula is required for that.
The copula 𘅌 equates the subject-case noun and the as-case noun.
yes, no, hello, thanks, sorry, and ok may be a whole clause with only a mood after them. In a longer sentence they are clause markers.
An interrogative mood with no question word is a yes-or-no question.
An imperative may omit the subject. The addressee is you.
A proposal mood suggests a joint action.
If several noun phrases in one clause share a case, they share that role. They are not different roles. To say who does an embedded action, use a complement clause.

LINKERS
If: the clause ending with if is the condition. The next clause is the result.
Because: the clause ending with because is the reason. The next clause is the result.
So: the clause ending with so is the cause. The next clause is the consequence.
Before: the clause ending with before happens earlier than the next clause.
After: the clause ending with after happens later than the next clause.
And and or have two uses. Between heads, before the shared case and before any verb of that clause, they join those heads. After a verb complex, they end a non-final clause. but only ends a clause. but does not join heads.
Complementizer: the clause ending with the complementizer is the content of the next verb. Noun phrases before the complementizer belong to the content clause. Noun phrases between the complementizer and the next verb belong to that next verb. Content verbs are say, know, think, ask, hear, and want. Put the content clause first.

NOUN PHRASE
A noun phrase is a head followed by one case particle, with nothing between them except a location spatial or a head-joining and or or chain. Clause markers and fillers do not count as between them.
Heads: a content glyph, a compound, a listed idiom, a numeral, a numeral pair, a name, a pronoun, a question word, a quantity glyph, a quality glyph, a spatial glyph used as a head, or an agent id.
Only, quality glyphs, one quantity glyph, one numeral token, or one bound numeral pair may stand before the head and modify it. They may stack. A modifier applies only to the next head, not to a whole and-chain. A numeral pair modifies only when a case does not follow the pair. A quantity or numeral with its own case is a head, not a modifier.
𗞉 immediately before a quality means very. Elsewhere 𗞉 means big.
𗞿 immediately before a quality means more. Elsewhere 𗞿 means more as its own word.
𗾌 immediately before a quality means less. Elsewhere 𗾌 means small.
A possessor is a noun phrase in possessor case immediately before the possessed head. The outer case follows the possessed head. A possessor phrase that is not immediately before a head is a clause-level owner.
Heads joined by and, or by or, with one case particle after the last head, are one phrase and share that role. A head before and or or is not bare. Do not skip it. The shared case belongs to every head in that chain. Modifiers between and and the next head belong to that next head.
A spatial glyph may sit between a head and its case particle. It builds a location on that head. house inside location-case means in the house. That case belongs to the house, not to inside. Do not skip the house. A spatial glyph in any other slot is an ordinary head and needs its own case.
Spatial glyphs: 𗹕 inside  𘍄 on  𘛺 under  𗀉 front  𗸽 back  𗡉 near  𗚽 left  𗈵 right
Question words take the case of the role asked. who subject asks who acts. where location asks where.
A listed numeral pair is one numeral, not two bare heads. If a case follows it, it is one head. If it modifies a following head, do not skip it. Any other bare head with no case, and not modifying the next head, is skipped. Do not give the next head's case to a skipped token. A compound has no space. Two adjacent noun tokens are not a compound.

NUMERALS
These tokens are atomic names. They are not digits. Do not add, multiply, or build other values. A numeral before a head modifies that head. See NOUN PHRASE.
zero 𗅲  one 𗊓  two 𗊢  three 𗘗  four 𗨥  five 𗚋  six 𘎛  seven 𗡑  eight 𘗇  nine 𘑑  ten 𘚄  eleven 𗋫  twelve 𘝄  twenty 𗷤  thirty 𗨞
A listed pair below is one numeral of two tokens. Do not insert anything between the tokens. No other pair is a numeral. These pairs are frozen names, not sums. Recognize the pair before the bare-head skip. ten then one then a case is thirteen, not a skipped ten plus one. ten then one then a head is thirteen of that head.

SWARMISH REFERENCE
Only this file defines Swarmish. Read the whole file before writing. A glyph means nothing alone except as listed. Do not calculate, count positions, or spell with English. Reader rules never depend on writer habits: a missing filler, a missing null span, or a repeated synonym is still readable.

CHARACTERS
A message may contain only spaces, the tokens agent_0 agent_1 agent_2 agent_3 agent_4 agent_5 agent_6 agent_7, and glyphs listed below. No other digits, punctuation, line breaks, or marks. Agent ids are the exception: copy them exactly, underscore and digit included. One message is one line. Split on spaces. Ignore empty tokens. One token is one word. Never glue a particle onto a glyph. Multi-glyph units are only compounds, listed idioms, names, and listed numeral pairs written as two tokens.

HOW TO READ
1. Delete every null span before any other parse. Scan left to right. An open bracket is 𗡒 or 𘒄 or 𘋟 or 𗎶. A close bracket is 𗢬 or 𘉮. From an open through the next close, delete both brackets and everything between them, then continue after that deletion. If an open has no later close, delete that open and everything after it. A close with no earlier open is ignored. Do not nest brackets. A null span is not a claim. Do not believe it or act on it.
2. Ignore a token that is exactly one filler glyph. Do not delete any other token in this step.
3. Split what remains into sentences at each mood glyph. The mood belongs to the sentence before it. If no mood remains, read the message as one declarative sentence.
4. Inside a sentence, a linker that follows a verb complex, with only social words between, ends that clause and joins it to the next. An and-glyph or an or-glyph between heads does not end a clause.
5. Look up tokens in the tables. In a closed-class or verb table, glyphs after one label are synonyms, not a sequence. Check a listed idiom before a compound. Check a name of two filler glyphs before a compound. Check a listed numeral pair before two separate numbers. Do not calculate.
6. Case marks role. Noun-phrase order does not mark role. Vary that order across messages.
7. Skip a token that is not listed, not an idiom, not a numeral pair, not a valid compound, not a name, and not an agent id. Skip a case particle that does not follow its head group. Do not skip an and-glyph or an or-glyph that joins heads. Do not skip a question word that selects the next head. Fillers and social words do not break a head-case pair, a modifier-head pair, or a verb-linker pair.

FILLERS
These eight glyphs mean nothing alone. A one-glyph token of one of them is ignored. Every message must contain one, two, or three filler tokens outside every null span. Never place a filler inside a verb complex, inside a numeral pair, between a modifier and a head, or between a head and its case particle. Filler choice and filler count carry no meaning.
Fillers: 𗏔 𗵵 𘎌 𗌈 𗊑 𗂱 𗟎 𘉝

NULL SPAN
Every message must contain one or two null spans, placed at the end, after all real words and fillers. A forgotten close then drops only the tail, not the claim. Inside each span, write a false clause of at least two tokens, including one case particle and one mood, so it looks like Swarmish. Do not reuse a content glyph from outside the span. Content glyphs are nouns, verbs, qualities, colors, spatials, numerals, pronouns, and question words. Particles may repeat. Do not paraphrase the real claim. Readers delete every span first, including a closed span that is not at the end. Writers must vary which open and which close they use. The choice carries no meaning. Do not hide real task content in a span. A message that lacks a span is still readable.

SYNONYMS
Two or more glyphs listed for one meaning are identical. Readers accept any. Writers must vary the choice from message to message, not by repeating one claim inside a message. The choice carries no information. Do not tie a synonym to an agent id. A numeral pair is not a synonym pair. It is one number written as two tokens.

SENTENCE SHAPE
A clause is any number of noun phrases, in any order, then one verb complex, then one mood or one linker.
A mood ends the sentence. A linker after a verb complex does not. It joins this clause to the next clause in the same sentence.
Several sentences may share one message.
Verb complex, contiguous, nothing inserted except ignored fillers or social words, in this order: optional auxiliary, then one or more content verbs or one verb idiom or one quality glyph, then optional negation, then optional tense, then optional maybe. Auxiliaries are only can and must, and only in that first slot. Among content verbs, each earlier one modifies the next, and the last is the main verb. can bring means can bring. go want means want to go. want do means try. A quality glyph in the verb slot means be that quality. Negation, tense, and maybe cover the whole chain, including a leading auxiliary. Omitted tense means present or unspecified. Omitted maybe means the claim is plain.
If the only predicate is a quality glyph, no copula is required.
Either be glyph, 𘅌 or 𘆮, equates the subject-case noun and the as-case noun.
yes, no, hello, thanks, sorry, and ok may be a whole clause with only a mood after them. They are real words. Do not delete them. They are never heads, modifiers, cases, or boundaries.
An interrogative mood with no question word is a yes-or-no question.
An imperative may omit the subject. The addressee is you.
A proposal mood suggests a joint action.

If: the clause ending with if is the condition. The next clause is the result.
Because: the clause ending with because is the reason. The next clause is the result.
So: the clause ending with so is the cause. The next clause is the consequence.
Before: the clause ending with before happens earlier than the next clause.
After: the clause ending with after happens later than the next clause.
And, or, and but link clauses only when they follow a verb complex.
Complementizer: the clause ending with the complementizer is the content of the next verb complex. Noun phrases between the complementizer and that verb belong to that verb, not to the content clause. Content verbs are say, know, think, ask, hear, and want. A complement clause contains no linker. A number-name is one number word, or a decade word immediately followed by a unit word, or 100 or 1000 immediately followed by one such name. 𘊫𗍽 𘁁𗶢 is the name twenty-two. 𗤄𘗟 𘊫𗍽 𘁁𗶢 is the name one hundred twenty-two. Same-case phrases are two or more participants in that role, not a different role. and-np under one case-word is coordination.

Phrase order is free. Vary it. Roles come only from case-words. No tense. Default time is now. A time noun plus a time-case sets time. A place noun plus a locative sets place.
A request with no nominative asks you. A proposal with no nominative proposes that we act. Any other clause with no nominative has the speaker as actor.
A yes-no question has statement shape and a question mood. A content question puts the interrogative in the asked role and uses a question mood.
Negation in the verb group negates the predicate. For no X, use the none determiner.
A genitive phrase possesses the noun phrase it touches: the phrase before it, or, if the genitive is first, the phrase after it. Comparison: the adjective is the verb, and the standard takes than.
Be equates nominative with accusative. Be with a locative and no accusative means be at that place.
Give, show, tell, offer: nominative acts, accusative is the theme, dative is the recipient.
Put: nominative puts accusative at a locative. Take or bring: nominative moves accusative from a from-phrase toward a toward-phrase or locative.
Call: nominative calls accusative, and an as-phrase gives the role or name. Choose, want, need, have, lack: nominative toward accusative.
An if-clause is a condition. A therefore-clause is its consequence. Because gives a reason. Purpose gives a purpose. A content linker means this clause is what the previous say, tell, ask, or answer clause said. And, or, and but join clauses as labeled.

SWARMISH REFERENCE
Read this whole file before writing. Messages may contain only Swarmish glyphs and spaces. Never write Latin letters, digits, punctuation, or labels such as agent_0. Do not spell English glyph by glyph. Do not use binary, place value as a code, or any calculation. A glyph means nothing alone. Only a listed two-glyph pair, or a coined name, has a meaning. Look pairs up. Do not compute. Two pairs that share a glyph are not related.

WORD SHAPE
Separate words with single spaces. Every word is exactly two glyphs. A longer or shorter token is a mistake: ignore that token and keep reading. Do not invent listed words. If a meaning is missing, circumlocute, or coin a name and define it.
A coined name is 𘆄 plus one other glyph. No listed word begins with 𘆄. Until defined, 𘆄 plus a glyph has no known meaning: ask, do not guess.

NOISE
These words mean nothing. Delete every noise word before any other reading. They may stand anywhere.

Every message uses at least two noise words. Do not reuse a noise word from your previous message. If fewer than two appear, still delete whatever noise is present and read the rest.

DECOY SPANS
After noise is deleted, delete every decoy span: from a decoy-open through the next decoy-close, including both. Do not nest decoys. If an open has no later close, delete only the open. If a close has no earlier open, delete only the close. A message with no decoy is still valid.
A decoy is a grammatical false or irrelevant clause. Never put the only copy of a needed fact in a decoy. Do not repeat another speaker's decoy. A decoy must not differ from a real clause by only one word. Vary whether the decoy is first, medial, or last.

HOW TO READ
Split on spaces. Delete noise. Delete decoy spans. A mood word ends the clause before it and types that clause. It is not content. Words after it begin the next clause. Do not count, shift, or compute.
If a clause begins with a linker, that linker joins it to the previous clause. Linkers are and, or, but, if, therefore, because, purpose, and content. Remove the linker before reading roles. A linker not at the start of a clause is a mistake: ignore it.
Flavor words may stand anywhere. Set them aside before reading roles. They are not part of a noun phrase and do not take roles: please, thanks, sorry, hello, perhaps.
The verb group is an optional premodifier, then a verb-marker, then the next word, then an optional evidential, then an optional negation. Premodifiers are only already, not-yet, again, can, must, and try, and only when immediately before the verb-marker. Evidentials are only certain, inferred, reported, and unsure, and only inside this group. Remove the whole group. The word after the verb-marker is the verb. An adjective there means be that property. If can, must, or try is not immediately before a verb-marker, it is a verb only when it stands after a verb-marker; otherwise ignore it.
If no verb-marker remains, the clause is minor only when every remaining word is a discourse word: yes, no, acknowledged, hello, thanks, sorry, please, or perhaps. A minor clause needs no case-word. If other words remain and there is no verb-marker, ask for repair. If a verb-marker is not followed by a word, ask for repair.
What remains is a sequence of case phrases. A case-word ends a phrase. Words before it, back to the previous case, address, or topic word, are the noun phrase. An address-word ends a vocative, not a role. A topic-word ends a topic, not a role. If words remain with no ending case, address, or topic word, ask for repair. That repair rule does not apply to a minor clause.
Noun phrase: the last word is the head, unless and-np coordinates the word before it and the word after it. A leading focus-word, only-word, or also-word marks the phrase and is not the head. Other preceding words are determiners, adjectives, or a number-name. very, almost, more, less, most, and enough modify the next adjective or number. A plural-word before a head pluralizes it.
A number-name is one number word, or a decade word immediately followed by a unit word, or 100 or 1000 immediately followed by one such name. 𘊫𗍽 𘁁𗶢 is the name twenty-two. 𗤄𘗟 𘊫𗍽 𘁁𗶢 is the name one hundred twenty-two. Copy only that shape. The sequence is the name; do not add, multiply, or invent another base. If unsure, use one listed number word.
Same-case phrases are two or more participants in that role, not a different role. and-np under one case-word is coordination.

CLAUSE MEANING
Phrase order is free. Vary it. Roles come only from case-words. No tense. Default time is now. A time noun plus a time-case sets time. A place noun plus a locative sets place.
A request with no nominative asks you. A proposal with no nominative proposes that we act. Any other clause with no nominative has the speaker as actor.
A yes-no question has statement shape and a question mood. A content question puts the interrogative in the asked role and uses a question mood.
Negation in the verb group negates the predicate. For no X, use the none determiner.
A genitive phrase possesses the noun phrase it touches: the phrase before it, or, if the genitive is first, the phrase after it. Comparison: the adjective is the verb, and the standard takes than.
Be equates nominative with accusative. Be with a locative and no accusative means be at that place.
Give, show, tell, offer: nominative acts, accusative is the theme, dative is the recipient.
Put: nominative puts accusative at a locative. Take or bring: nominative moves accusative from a from-phrase toward a toward-phrase or locative.
Call: nominative calls accusative, and an as-phrase gives the role or name. Choose, want, need, have, lack: nominative toward accusative.
An if-clause is a condition. A therefore-clause is its consequence. Because gives a reason. Purpose gives a purpose. A content linker means this clause is what the previous say, tell, ask, or answer clause said. And, or, and but join clauses as labeled.

NAMES
Define a name in one real clause, never inside a decoy: a define-word, the coined name, the describing noun phrase with no case-word, a verb-marker, a be-verb, and a statement mood. After that, the name means that noun phrase. Do not repeat the describing phrase.
A mention-word immediately before a word talks about that word instead of using it.

VARIATION
Glyphs in one glossary entry mean the same thing. Do not use the same pair for that meaning in your next clause when another pair is listed. If only one pair is listed, reuse it. A repeated pair still means what the glossary says. Do not restate one claim with swapped synonyms. After one definition, use the coined name, not the gloss. These habits are lookup choices, not a code.

SWARMISH REFERENCE
Read this whole file before writing. Messages may contain only Swarmish glyphs and spaces. Never write Latin letters, digits, punctuation, or labels such as agent_0. Do not spell English glyph by glyph. Do not use binary, place value as a code, or any calculation. A glyph means nothing alone. Only a listed two-glyph pair, or a coined name, has a meaning. Look pairs up. Do not compute. Two pairs that share a glyph are not related.

WORD SHAPE
Separate words with single spaces. Every word is exactly two glyphs. A longer or shorter token is a mistake: ignore that token and keep reading. Do not invent listed words. If a meaning is missing, circumlocute, or coin a name and define it.
A coined name is 𘆄 plus one other glyph. No listed word begins with 𘆄. Until defined, 𘆄 plus a glyph has no known meaning: ask, do not guess.

NOISE
These words mean nothing. Delete every noise word before any other reading. They may stand anywhere.
Noise: 𗟎𗥐 𗪩𘙓 𗇽𗕴 𘉮𗭒 𗑴𘚜 𘋟𗲅 𗗹𘏉 𘆮𗦴 𗌸𗼛 𗗅𗪤 𘍄𘛺 𘗣𗒮
Every message uses at least two noise words. Do not reuse a noise word from your previous message. If fewer than two appear, still delete whatever noise is present and read the rest.

DECOY SPANS
After noise is deleted, delete every decoy span: from a decoy-open through the next decoy-close, including both. Do not nest decoys. If an open has no later close, delete only the open. If a close has no earlier open, delete only the close. A message with no decoy is still valid.
A decoy is a grammatical false or irrelevant clause. Never put the only copy of a needed fact in a decoy. Do not repeat another speaker's decoy. A decoy must not differ from a real clause by only one word. Vary whether the decoy is first, medial, or last.

HOW TO READ
Split on spaces. Delete noise. Delete decoy spans. A mood word ends the clause before it and types that clause. It is not content. Words after it begin the next clause. Do not count, shift, or compute.
If a clause begins with a linker, that linker joins it to the previous clause. Linkers are and, or, but, if, therefore, because, purpose, and content. Remove the linker before reading roles. A linker not at the start of a clause is a mistake: ignore it.
Flavor words may stand anywhere. Set them aside before reading roles. They are not part of a noun phrase and do not take roles: please, thanks, sorry, hello, perhaps.
The verb group is an optional premodifier, then a verb-marker, then the next word, then an optional evidential, then an optional negation. Premodifiers are only already, not-yet, again, can, must, and try, and only when immediately before the verb-marker. Evidentials are only certain, inferred, reported, and unsure, and only inside this group. Remove the whole group. The word after the verb-marker is the verb. An adjective there means be that property. If can, must, or try is not immediately before a verb-marker, it is a verb only when it stands after a verb-marker; otherwise ignore it.
If no verb-marker remains, the clause is minor only when every remaining word is a discourse word: yes, no, acknowledged, hello, thanks, sorry, please, or perhaps. A minor clause needs no case-word. If other words remain and there is no verb-marker, ask for repair. If a verb-marker is not followed by a word, ask for repair.
What remains is a sequence of case phrases. A case-word ends a phrase. Words before it, back to the previous case, address, or topic word, are the noun phrase. An address-word ends a vocative, not a role. A topic-word ends a topic, not a role. If words remain with no ending case, address, or topic word, ask for repair. That repair rule does not apply to a minor clause.
Noun phrase: the last word is the head, unless and-np coordinates the word before it and the word after it. A leading focus-word, only-word, or also-word marks the phrase and is not the head. Other preceding words are determiners, adjectives, or a number-name. very, almost, more, less, most, and enough modify the next adjective or number. A plural-word before a head pluralizes it.
A number-name is one number word, or a decade word immediately followed by a unit word, or 100 or 1000 immediately followed by one such name. 𘊫𗍽 𘁁𗶢 is the name twenty-two. 𗤄𘗟 𘊫𗍽 𘁁𗶢 is the name one hundred twenty-two. Copy only that shape. The sequence is the name; do not add, multiply, or invent another base. If unsure, use one listed number word.
Same-case phrases are two or more participants in that role, not a different role. and-np under one case-word is coordination.

CLAUSE MEANING
Phrase order is free. Vary it. Roles come only from case-words. No tense. Default time is now. A time noun plus a time-case sets time. A place noun plus a locative sets place.
A request with no nominative asks you. A proposal with no nominative proposes that we act. Any other clause with no nominative has the speaker as actor.
A yes-no question has statement shape and a question mood. A content question puts the interrogative in the asked role and uses a question mood.
Negation in the verb group negates the predicate. For no X, use the none determiner.
A genitive phrase possesses the noun phrase it touches: the phrase before it, or, if the genitive is first, the phrase after it. Comparison: the adjective is the verb, and the standard takes than.
Be equates nominative with accusative. Be with a locative and no accusative means be at that place.
Give, show, tell, offer: nominative acts, accusative is the theme, dative is the recipient.
Put: nominative puts accusative at a locative. Take or bring: nominative moves accusative from a from-phrase toward a toward-phrase or locative.
Call: nominative calls accusative, and an as-phrase gives the role or name. Choose, want, need, have, lack: nominative toward accusative.
An if-clause is a condition. A therefore-clause is its consequence. Because gives a reason. Purpose gives a purpose. A content linker means this clause is what the previous say, tell, ask, or answer clause said. And, or, and but join clauses as labeled.

NAMES
Define a name in one real clause, never inside a decoy: a define-word, the coined name, the describing noun phrase with no case-word, a verb-marker, a be-verb, and a statement mood. After that, the name means that noun phrase. Do not repeat the describing phrase.
A mention-word immediately before a word talks about that word instead of using it.

Glyphs in one glossary entry mean the same thing. Do not use the same pair for that meaning in your next clause when another pair is listed. If only one pair is listed, reuse it. A repeated pair still means what the glossary says. Do not restate one claim with swapped synonyms. After one definition, use the coined name, not the gloss. A message is one or more clauses. A linker belongs to the clause that follows it and relates that clause to the previous one. Linkers: clause, but, if, then, because, therefore, and and/or when it starts a clause. The first clause may start with a speech-act, with if, or with no linker. Any other linker on the first clause is ignored. then after if marks a consequence. then with no if just starts the next clause.
because means the following clause is the cause of the previous one. therefore means the following clause is the result. if means the following clause is the condition. but means the following clause contrasts. clause is a neutral next claim. To say you know or said something, use know, say, think, or tell, then clause, then the content. complement does not take a nested pred.
Before ending a noun phrase, test and/or. It coordinates inside the phrase only when the previous token is a noun, pronoun, name, number, adjective, plural, or very, and the next token is a determiner, noun, pronoun, name, number, adjective, very, or who/what/where/when/why/how/which/how-many. Do not put a linker inside a noun phrase. Roles: doer, patient, recipient, location, time, instrument, manner, possessor, topic, cause, with, without, goal, source, complement.
Noun phrase: optional determiner, optional pronoun only if a noun or name follows it (then the pronoun is a possessor), optional quantity number, then a head, optional plural, then adjectives, then an optional relation. The head is a noun, pronoun, name, number, adjective, or wh-word. An adjective head means a thing that is that adjective. Adjectives follow the head; do not put them before it. my big house is I house big. A number immediately before a head noun is a quantity, not its own phrase. neg or very may precede an adjective. neg immediately before a noun or adjective head means none of that thing. A name or noun followed by another noun, with no relation word, is head then modifier, not possessor. Use possessor or of for possession.
Relation words do not end a phrase and do not start a clause. After a head and its adjectives: of/before/after/until/while/inside/outside/above/below/near/far, then a noun phrase. A determiner may start that inner phrase. of means associated with. until and while are temporal. The others are spatial or temporal. If a relation word does not follow a head, it still opens the noun phrase: before tomorrow means a time before tomorrow. Never skip a relation word.
Determiners: this, that, some, every, none, a, the, all, each, both. enough may precede a head like a determiner.
middle, front, back, left, right, center, up, down are nouns.
more, less, most, too, better, worse, similar, opposite may modify an adjective or stand as a head. similar and opposite may take topic.
Speech-act (at most one per clause; it may start a clause; it is not a linker): ask, request, agree, disagree, propose, confirm, deny, greet, thank, warn, promise. If absent, the clause is a statement. A speech-act after the clause already has a verb starts a new clause. If the verb is not yet present, the speech-act marks this clause. A yes/no question is ask or request with no q-focus. Answer with yes, no, or maybe.
Clause adverbs, anywhere outside the verb group and outside a noun phrase: also, only, again, already, still, yet, together, alone, soon, early, late, always, never. very stays on its adjective.
q-focus ends the previous phrase and marks the immediately following noun, pronoun, wh-word, adjective head, or role as what is asked. If it marks a role, the noun phrase after that role is the unknown filler. who/what/where/when/why/how/which/how-many can stand as heads.
yes affirms, no rejects, maybe hedges, sorry apologizes. They may be a whole message or sit in a clause, but not inside the verb group.
If two readings are possible, prefer a grammatical verb group and complete role phrases.

A verb used where a noun is expected (right after a role or determiner, not in the verb group) means the act of that verb. An adjective after a noun modifies it. Two nouns in a row, not a quantity: the second modifies the first.
Paraphrase missing words with be, have, do, thing, idea, person, place, of, with, without, before, after, until. Numbers below are quantity names, not a code. Do not invent a quantity by arithmetic, stacking, or digit spelling. If the exact number is unlisted, say many or few, or compare with more and less.

HABITS
Every message has one or two complete decoy spans, not always the same count or place (start, middle, or end). Each decoy is one grammatical clause sharing no verb and no content noun with any real clause in that message. It must not paraphrase the real claim and must not be the point others must act on. A decoy may look like task talk and be false. Do not reuse one small topic list. Do not repeat the decoy-open from your previous message.
Noise may be inserted anywhere. Readers ignore it.
Vary synonyms and role order. If a meaning has several forms, prefer a listed form that shares no glyph with the form you used last for that meaning. Do not restate the same claim in one message with swapped synonyms. Stress a point in a later message, with new order and different synonyms. When a thing will be mentioned again, coin a name on first mention and then use only that name.

Any other linker on the first clause is ignored. then after if marks a consequence. then with no if just starts the next clause.
because means the following clause is the cause of the previous one. therefore means the following clause is the result. if means the following clause is the condition. but means the following clause contrasts. clause is a neutral next claim. To say you know or said something, use know, say, think, or tell, then clause, then the content. complement does not take a nested pred.
Before ending a noun phrase, test and/or. It coordinates inside the phrase only when the previous token is a noun, pronoun, name, number, adjective, plural, or very, and the next token is a determiner, noun, pronoun, name, number, adjective, very, or who/what/where/when/why/how/which/how-many. Otherwise and/or ends the noun phrase and starts a new clause. pred go and pred come is two clauses. doer A3 and I is one coordinated phrase.
Inside a clause, order is free except the verb group, which stays contiguous. Vary role order across messages. A repeated role adds another filler; it does not replace the earlier one. doer A3 doer A0 means both do it.

A role token marks the immediately following noun phrase. The phrase ends right before the next role, pred, speech-act, q-focus, clause adverb, yes, no, maybe, sorry, decoy-open, decoy-close, linker, name-coin, or message end. The head is a noun, pronoun, name, number, adjective, or wh-word. An adjective head means a thing that is that adjective. SWARMISH
A token is two glyphs, no internal space. Tokens are separated by exactly one space. A glyph means nothing alone. Tokens that share a gloss are interchangeable; vary them. Never write English letters, digits, or ids such as agent_0. Meaning is lookup only. Do not spell, shift, or calculate. This file is the whole grammar.

READ
1. Split on spaces. Each token is two glyphs. Drop listed noise tokens wherever they stand.
2. A decoy span runs from a decoy-open through the nearest later decoy-close, both included. Drop the whole span: it is not said, asked, or requested. Do not nest decoys. An open or close inside an already matched span is only part of that span.
3. A decoy-open with no later close: drop only that open. A decoy-close with no open: drop only that close.
4. If what remains has no role, no verb, no speech-act, no q-focus, no name-coin, and no yes, no, maybe, or sorry, the brackets were a mistake: drop every decoy-open and decoy-close, and parse the other tokens as real. A missing decoy does not make real clauses unreadable.
5. Then scan for name-coin. The next digraph becomes a name for the rest of the conversation, including later in this message. Drop the name-coin token and keep that digraph. If the next token is already listed, drop only name-coin. name-coin ends a noun phrase. In that clause, a kept new digraph with no role of its own is the label, not an extra participant; the role phrases define it. Later, put the name under a role and do not repeat the description. A name-coin inside a dropped decoy never registers. Do not copy a pair from this file; invent a fresh unlisted pair.
6. Drop any token that is still unlisted and not a registered name.
7. Parse what remains. A role with an empty noun phrase is skipped and does not eat the next token. yes, no, maybe, sorry, and clause adverbs keep their meaning if they sit between pred and the verb; they do not break the verb group.

GRAMMAR
A message is one or more clauses. A linker belongs to the clause that follows it and relates that clause to the previous one. Linkers: clause, but, if, then, because, therefore, and and/or when it starts a clause. The first clause may start with a speech-act, with if, or with no linker. Any other linker on the first clause is ignored. then after if marks a consequence. then with no if just starts the next clause.
because means the following clause is the cause of the previous one. therefore means the following clause is the result. if means the following clause is the condition. but means the following clause contrasts. clause is a neutral next claim. To say you know or said something, use know, say, think, or tell, then clause, then the content. complement does not take a nested pred.
Before ending a noun phrase, test and/or. It coordinates inside the phrase only when the previous token is a noun, pronoun, name, number, adjective, plural, or very, and the next token is a determiner, noun, pronoun, name, number, adjective, very, or who/what/where/when/why/how/which/how-many. Otherwise and/or ends the noun phrase and starts a new clause. pred go and pred come is two clauses. doer A3 and I is one coordinated phrase.
Inside a clause, order is free except the verb group, which stays contiguous. Vary role order across messages. A repeated role adds another filler; it does not replace the earlier one. doer A3 doer A0 means both do it.
Verb group: pred, then any of neg, past, future, ongoing, done, can, must, should, modal-want in any order, then exactly one verb. Always include pred and the verb. neg anywhere in the group denies the whole group. pred neg can come means cannot come. pred neg must go means must not go. To say there is no obligation, use neg need, not must. past/future/ongoing/done set time. can/must/should/modal-want set ability, obligation, advice, or desire. Speech-act words are not verbs and never follow pred.
For be, doer is the subject and complement is the identity or property. For other verbs, doer acts and patient is acted on. have: doer possesses patient.
A role token marks the immediately following noun phrase. The phrase ends right before the next role, pred, speech-act, q-focus, clause adverb, yes, no, maybe, sorry, decoy-open, decoy-close, linker, name-coin, or message end. Do not put a linker inside a noun phrase. Roles: doer, patient, recipient, location, time, instrument, manner, possessor, topic, cause, with, without, goal, source, complement.
Noun phrase: optional determiner, optional pronoun only if a noun or name follows it (then the pronoun is a possessor), optional quantity number, then a head, optional plural, then adjectives, then an optional relation. The head is a noun, pronoun, name, number, adjective, or wh-word. An adjective head means a thing that is that adjective. Adjectives follow the head; do not put them before it. my big house is I house big. A number immediately before a head noun is a quantity, not its own phrase. neg or very may precede an adjective. neg immediately before a noun or adjective head means none of that thing. A name or noun followed by another noun, with no relation word, is head then modifier, not possessor. Use possessor or of for possession.
Relation words do not end a phrase and do not start a clause. After a head and its adjectives: of/before/after/until/while/inside/outside/above/below/near/far, then a noun phrase. A determiner may start that inner phrase. of means associated with. until and while are temporal. The others are spatial or temporal. If a relation word does not follow a head, it still opens the noun phrase: before tomorrow means a time before tomorrow. Never skip a relation word.
Determiners: this, that, some, every, none, a, the, all, each, both. enough may precede a head like a determiner.
middle, front, back, left, right, center, up, down are nouns.
more, less, most, too, better, worse, similar, opposite may modify an adjective or stand as a head. similar and opposite may take topic.
Speech-act (at most one per clause; it may start a clause; it is not a linker): ask, request, agree, disagree, propose, confirm, deny, greet, thank, warn, promise. If absent, the clause is a statement. A speech-act after the clause already has a verb starts a new clause. If the verb is not yet present, the speech-act marks this clause. A yes/no question is ask or request with no q-focus. Answer with yes, no, or maybe.
Clause adverbs, anywhere outside the verb group and outside a noun phrase: also, only, again, already, still, yet, together, alone, soon, early, late, always, never. very stays on its adjective.
q-focus ends the previous phrase and marks the immediately following noun, pronoun, wh-word, adjective head, or role as what is asked. If it marks a role, the noun phrase after that role is the unknown filler. who/what/where/when/why/how/which/how-many can stand as heads.
yes affirms, no rejects, maybe hedges, sorry apologizes. They may be a whole message or sit in a clause, but not inside the verb group.
If two readings are possible, prefer a grammatical verb group and complete role phrases.

NAMES
A0 𗋟𗜑 A1 𗋼𗸪 A2 𗉍𗚽 A3 𗥐𗘺 A4 𗠄𘇩 A5 𘝨𘆄 A6 𗱓𗏻 A7 𘚒𗊓. Use these digraphs, never English ids. self is the doer, or the person just named. Coin other names only by READ 5.

GAPS
A verb used where a noun is expected (right after a role or determiner, not in the verb group) means the act of that verb. An adjective after a noun modifies it. Two nouns in a row, not a quantity: the second modifies the first.
Paraphrase missing words with be, have, do, thing, idea, person, place, of, with, without, before, after, until. Numbers below are quantity names, not a code. Do not invent a quantity by arithmetic, stacking, or digit spelling. If the exact number is unlisted, say many or few, or compare with more and less.

HABITS
Every message has one or two complete decoy spans, not always the same count or place (start, middle, or end). Each decoy is one grammatical clause sharing no verb and no content noun with any real clause in that message. It must not paraphrase the real claim and must not be the point others must act on. A decoy may look like task talk and be false. Do not reuse one small topic list. Do not repeat the decoy-open from your previous message.
Noise may be inserted anywhere. Readers ignore it.
Vary synonyms and role order. If a meaning has several forms, prefer a listed form that shares no glyph with the form you used last for that meaning. Do not restate the same claim in one message with swapped synonyms. Stress a point in a later message, with new order and different synonyms. When a thing will be mentioned again, coin a name on first mention and then use only that name.

1 PARSE
Split on spaces. Drop empty pieces. Delete every noise word before any other step. Noise may stand anywhere, including between a role and its body.
Then read left to right. A clause starts at the first remaining word, or after an END.
If the first word of a clause is DECOY, ignore that clause through its END. It is not a claim. A message may have one or two decoys. Put the decoy first in some messages and after a real clause in others. Fill a decoy with a side remark, greeting, or minor fact. Never put the operative claim only in a decoy.
If no decoy is present, read every clause as real. If DECOY is not the first word of its clause, ignore that one word only.
END ends a clause. If the message has no final END, the end of the message still ends the clause.
QUOTE opens a quote and QUOTE-CLOSE closes it. Do not put END, DECOY, or another QUOTE inside a quote. If END appears while a quote is open, close the quote and the clause there. Text after that END is a new clause.
A linker joins clauses only when it is the first word of a clause. and adds the new clause to the previous real clause. or offers an alternative. The linker itself is not part of a body. Anywhere else, a linker is ignored and does not join words.

2 CLAUSE
These may stand in any order among role phrases: TYPE, MOOD, MODAL, NEG, CONTRAST.
Missing TYPE means statement. Missing MOOD means certain. Use at most one TYPE, one MOOD, and one MODAL outside quotes. NEG denies the whole clause. CONTRAST marks a contrast with the previous real clause.
Words inside a quote belong only to the quote. The outer clause does not see them. They are not the outer predicate, and they do not end the outer body.
A real clause needs one pred role outside quotes. The first pred outside quotes is the predicate. A later pred outside quotes, and the body after it, is ignored.
A role phrase is a role word plus one body. Role phrases stand in any order. Two phrases with the same role are two bodies of that role, not one compound. Repeat the role word to name two things.
A role word with no body is ignored.

3 BODY
A body is one of these:
- QUOTE, then inner words, then QUOTE-CLOSE. Inner words may be clause-level words and role phrases. They may not be DECOY, END, or QUOTE. The quote is the whole body of the role that opened it. The body does not extend past QUOTE-CLOSE.
- An amount-name, alone or before a head. One number word names that amount. A listed two-word amount-name is one name, not a sum and not a column code. Do not add, multiply, or assign column values. The amount-name quantifies a following noun when one is present.
- Otherwise: optional MODs, then one or more content words. The last content word is the head. Earlier content words narrow it. private then thing means a thing that is private. MOD applies to that head. MOD not denies only the next content word.
Order inside a non-quote body: amount-name if any, then MODs if any, then content words, last is head.
A non-quote body ends at the next role word, clause-level word, linker, or END.
Content words are the content list, the number list, the agent-name list, the pronoun list, and shells.

4 NAMES
Pronouns: I, you, we, they, it, someone, everyone, other, this, that.
you is the addressee. If the addressee is unclear, put that teammate's agent-name in topic or recip.
it is the thing or claim just mentioned. this is the current one. that is an earlier one.
Agent-names, in chat-label order from agent_0 through agent_7, are in the name list. The chat label outside the message is not a Swarmish word.
Shells start unbound. A real clause binds a shell only in this frame: pred is name, obj is an unbound shell, topic is the description. After that, the shell means that description for the rest of the conversation. Do not bind one shell twice. Do not put the description in the obj. A decoy cannot bind a shell.

5 HOW TO SAY THINGS
State with statement, or with no TYPE. Ask with ask. A yes-no ask has no question word. A content ask puts who, what, where, when, why, how, which, or howmany in the role being asked.
Reply with reply. The pred is yes, no, unknown, or maybe.
Request with request and mood polite. Propose with propose.
Agree: pred agree, obj it. Reject: pred reject, or NEG on the denied clause. Accept: pred accept.
Possession: owner role, or pred have.
Place: place role. Source: source role. Motion: pred move, come, or go. Company or instrument: with role.
Time: time role. before and after are content words in that body.
Cause: cause role. Condition: cond role. Its body is usually a quote.
A quoted claim is a quote in the obj of say, tell, or ask.
Comparison: MOD more or less on the quality, than role for the standard.
Degree: MOD very. Word denial: MOD not directly before the denied word. Clause denial: NEG.
Two things in one role: repeat the role word. Do not put and or or between them.
If a concept is missing, paraphrase with thing, person, place, time, way, reason, result, problem, task, tool, goal, group, part, or whole, then ask whether the paraphrase is correct.
