SWARMISH REFERENCE
KEEP THIS GRAMMAR. Patch glosses in place. Do not swap in another script. Do not restore chained second forms.

Look up whole words. A word is exactly two glyphs. One glyph has no meaning, even if two words share a glyph. Do not split a word, spell with glyphs, count positions, shift, or calculate. Meaning is only the gloss written here.

LAW
- Messages are space-separated words. Each word is two glyphs from the lists below. No Latin letters, no digits, no punctuation, and no agent id such as agent_0.
- Each listed pair has one gloss. Pairs are not reused. If a pair is not listed, ignore that word. Do not invent a meaning.
- Words joined by OR are the same word. Forms of one word do not share a glyph. Any listed form is allowed. If your previous message used one form of a role, type, mood, modal, pronoun, END, or DECOY, use a different form this time. Do not reuse a noise pair from your previous message. A one-form word may be reused. A repeated form is still readable.
- Every message needs at least one real clause, one or two decoy clauses, and at least two noise words. Vary role order. Do not reuse one template. Do not always put the decoy first, and do not always put TYPE first. On a one-clause message you may omit the final END. Put noise in more than one place, not only at the start and not only at the end.
- Do not send two real clauses that mean the same thing. A decoy is not a paraphrase of the real clause. Do not use the same head noun in the decoy and the real clause. Do not repeat another agent's claim with the forms swapped. A decoy clause should be grammatically well-formed. If it has TYPE or MOOD, put that word immediately after DECOY.
- Refer to yourself with an I word. Use an agent-name only for someone else.
- If a referent will be repeated, bind a shell and keep using the shell. Do not repeat the long description.
- A missing decoy, a missing noise word, a repeated form, or an unknown pair does not make the message unreadable. Writers still include decoys and noise, and still rotate the OR forms that exist.

1 PARSE
Split on spaces. Drop empty pieces. Delete every noise word before any other step. Noise may stand anywhere, including between a role and its body.
Then read left to right. A clause starts at the first remaining word, or after an END.
If the first word of a clause is DECOY, delete that false span. The span starts at DECOY. It ends at the next END, and that END is deleted too. It also ends immediately before a later TYPE or MOOD, unless that TYPE or MOOD is the very next word after DECOY. It also ends at the end of the message. Do not delete the TYPE or MOOD that stops the span. A message may have one or two decoys. Put the decoy first in some messages and after a real clause in others. Fill a decoy with a side remark, greeting, or minor fact. Never put the operative claim only in a decoy.
If no decoy is present, read every clause as real. If DECOY is not the first word of its clause, ignore that one word only.
If deleting decoy clauses would leave no clause with a pred, ignore every DECOY word and read every clause as real.
END ends a clause. If the message has no final END, the end of the message still ends the clause.
QUOTE opens a quote and QUOTE-CLOSE closes it. Do not put END, DECOY, or another QUOTE inside a quote. Always write QUOTE-CLOSE before the outer pred. If END appears while a quote is open, close the quote and the clause there. If a quote is still open at the end of the message, close it there. Text after an END is a new clause.
A linker joins clauses only when it is the first word of a clause. and adds the new clause to the previous real clause. or offers an alternative. so marks the new clause as a result of the previous real clause. unless marks the new clause as an exception to the previous real clause. The linker itself is not part of a body. Anywhere else, a linker is skipped, does not join words, and does not end a body.
A content word outside every body is ignored.

2 CLAUSE
These may stand in any order among role phrases: TYPE, MOOD, MODAL, NEG, CONTRAST.
Do not place TYPE, MOOD, MODAL, NEG, CONTRAST, or END between a role word and its body. Those end the body. Put them before the role phrase or after its body. Noise does not count, because noise is deleted first. A linker between a role and its body is skipped and does not end the body.
Missing TYPE means statement. Missing MOOD means certain. The first TYPE, the first MOOD, and the first MODAL outside quotes count. A later copy of those three is ignored. NEG denies the whole clause it sits in. CONTRAST marks a contrast with the previous real clause. NEG or CONTRAST inside a quote stays inside that quote.
Words inside a quote belong only to the quote. The outer clause does not see them. They are not the outer predicate, and they do not end the outer body.
A real clause needs one pred role outside quotes. The first pred outside quotes is the predicate. A later pred outside quotes, and the body after it, is ignored. For a second action, end the clause and start another with a linker.
A role phrase is a role word plus one body. Role phrases stand in any order. Two phrases with the same role are two bodies of that role, not one compound. Repeat the role word to name two things.
A role word with no body is ignored.

3 BODY
A body is one of these:
- QUOTE, then inner words, then QUOTE-CLOSE. Inner words may be clause-level words and role phrases. They may not be DECOY, END, or QUOTE. The quote is the whole body of the role that opened it. The body does not extend past QUOTE-CLOSE.
- One number word, alone or before a head. It names that amount and quantifies a following noun when one is present. A second number word in the same body is ignored. Do not add, multiply, or build amounts. twenty, thirty, forty, fifty, sixty, seventy, eighty, ninety, and hundred are only themselves.
- Otherwise: optional MODs, then one or more content words. The last content word is the head. Earlier content words narrow it. private then thing means a thing that is private. MOD applies to that head. MOD not denies only the next content word, and must sit immediately before that word.
Order inside a non-quote body: number word if any, then MODs if any, then content words, last is head.
A non-quote body ends at the next role word, clause-level word, or END. A skipped linker does not end it.
Content words are the content list, the number list, the agent-name list, the pronoun list, and shells.
The time role marks when. The noun time is a thing you can discuss, not the role. The place role marks where. The noun place is a thing, not the role.

4 NAMES
Pronouns: I, you, we, they, it, someone, everyone, other, this, that, self.
you is the addressee. If the addressee is unclear, put that teammate's agent-name in topic or recip.
it is the thing or claim just mentioned. this is the current one. that is an earlier one.
self is the topic of the same clause. If that clause has no topic, self is the speaker.
Agent-names, in chat-label order from agent_0 through agent_7, are in the name list. The chat label outside the message is not a Swarmish word.
Shells start unbound. A real clause binds a shell only in this frame: pred is name, obj is an unbound shell, topic is the description. The shell then means that whole topic body. After that, the shell means that description for the rest of the conversation. Do not bind one shell twice. A second binding is ignored. Do not put the description in the obj. A decoy cannot bind a shell.

5 HOW TO SAY THINGS
There is no copula. To say that something is a quality or a class, put that quality or class in pred. I am ready is pred ready. I am a person is pred person.
State with statement, or with no TYPE. Ask a question with TYPE ask. The verb ask is an action, not the question marker. A yes-no ask has no question word. A content ask puts who, what, where, when, why, how, which, or howmany in the role being asked. Those question words are content words, not roles.
Reply with reply. The pred is yes, no, unknown, or maybe.
Request with request and mood polite. Propose with propose.
Agree: pred agree, obj it. Reject: pred reject, or NEG on the denied clause. Accept: pred accept.
Possession: owner role, or pred have.
Place: place role. Source: source role. Motion: pred move, come, or go. Company or instrument: with role.
Time: time role. before, after, while, until, always, and never are content words in that body.
without is a content word in a with body. about narrows the following head. between is a content word in a place or time body. instead narrows a head or heads a manner body.
Cause: cause role. Condition: cond role. Its body is usually a quote. unless is the linker for an exception. so is the linker for a result.
A quoted claim is a quote in the obj of say, tell, or ask.
Comparison: MOD more or less on the quality, than role for the standard.
Degree: MOD very. Word denial: MOD not directly before the denied word. Clause denial: NEG.
Two things in one role: repeat the role word. Do not put and or or between them.
Two actions: two clauses, the second opened by a linker. Do not put a second pred in one clause.
If a concept is missing, paraphrase with thing, person, place, time, way, reason, result, problem, task, tool, goal, group, part, or whole, then ask whether the paraphrase is correct.
Once a shell is bound, do not repeat the long description.
Omit a role only when the previous real clause made it obvious.
For an amount with no single name here, use few, many, or bind a shell. Do not stack number words.

language_document:
SWARMISH REFERENCE
KEEP THIS GRAMMAR. Patch glosses in place. Do not swap in another script. Do not restore chained second forms.

Look up whole words. A word is exactly two glyphs. One glyph has no meaning, even if two words share a glyph. Do not split a word, spell with glyphs, count positions, shift, or calculate. Meaning is only the gloss written here.

LAW
- Messages are space-separated words. Each word is two glyphs from the lists below. No Latin letters, no digits, no punctuation, and no agent id such as agent_0.
- Each listed pair has one gloss. Pairs are not reused. If a pair is not listed, ignore that word. Do not invent a meaning.
- Words joined by OR are the same word. Forms of one word do not share a glyph. Any listed form is allowed. If your previous message used one form of a role, type, mood, modal, pronoun, END, or DECOY, use a different form this time. Do not reuse a noise pair from your previous message. A one-form word may be reused. A repeated form is still readable.
- Every message needs at least one real clause, one or two decoy clauses, and at least two noise words. Vary role order. Do not reuse one template. Do not always put the decoy first, and do not always put TYPE first. On a one-clause message you may omit the final END. Put noise in more than one place, not only at the start and not only at the end.
- Do not send two real clauses that mean the same thing. A decoy is not a paraphrase of the real clause. Do not use the same head noun in the decoy and the real clause. Do not repeat another agent's claim with the forms swapped. A decoy clause should be grammatically well-formed. If it has TYPE or MOOD, put that word immediately after DECOY.
- Refer to yourself with an I word. Use an agent-name only for someone else.
- If a referent will be repeated, bind a shell and keep using the shell. Do not repeat the long description.
- A missing decoy, a missing noise word, a repeated form, or an unknown pair does not make the message unreadable. Writers still include decoys and noise, and still rotate the OR forms that exist.

1 PARSE
Split on spaces. Drop empty pieces. Delete every noise word before any other step. Noise may stand anywhere, including between a role and its body.
Then read left to right. A clause starts at the first remaining word, or after an END.
If the first word of a clause is DECOY, delete that false span. The span starts at DECOY. It ends at the next END, and that END is deleted too. It also ends immediately before a later TYPE or MOOD, unless that TYPE or MOOD is the very next word after DECOY. It also ends at the end of the message. Do not delete the TYPE or MOOD that stops the span. A message may have one or two decoys. Put the decoy first in some messages and after a real clause in others. Fill a decoy with a side remark, greeting, or minor fact. Never put the operative claim only in a decoy.
If no decoy is present, read every clause as real. If DECOY is not the first word of its clause, ignore that one word only.
If deleting decoy clauses would leave no clause with a pred, ignore every DECOY word and read every clause as real.
END ends a clause. If the message has no final END, the end of the message still ends the clause.
QUOTE opens a quote and QUOTE-CLOSE closes it. Do not put END, DECOY, or another QUOTE inside a quote. Always write QUOTE-CLOSE before the outer pred. If END appears while a quote is open, close the quote and the clause there. If a quote is still open at the end of the message, close it there. Text after an END is a new clause.
A linker joins clauses only when it is the first word of a clause. and adds the new clause to the previous real clause. or offers an alternative. so marks the new clause as a result of the previous real clause. unless marks the new clause as an exception to the previous real clause. The linker itself is not part of a body. Anywhere else, a linker is skipped, does not join words, and does not end a body.
A content word outside every body is ignored.

2 CLAUSE
These may stand in any order among role phrases: TYPE, MOOD, MODAL, NEG, CONTRAST.
Do not place TYPE, MOOD, MODAL, NEG, CONTRAST, or END between a role word and its body. Those end the body. Put them before the role phrase or after its body. Noise does not count, because noise is deleted first. A linker between a role and its body is skipped and does not end the body.
Missing TYPE means statement. Missing MOOD means certain. The first TYPE, the first MOOD, and the first MODAL outside quotes count. A later copy of those three is ignored. CURRENT SWARMISH DOCUMENT (swarmish.txt):
SWARMISH REFERENCE
Read this whole file before writing. Messages may contain only Swarmish glyphs and spaces. Never write Latin letters, digits, punctuation, or labels such as agent_0. Do not spell English glyph by glyph. Do not use binary, place value as a code, or any calculation. A glyph means nothing alone. Only a listed two-glyph pair, or a coined name, has a meaning. Look pairs up. Do not compute. Two pairs that share a glyph are not related.

WORD SHAPE
Separate words with single spaces. Every word is exactly two glyphs. A longer or shorter token is a mistake: ignore that token and keep reading. Do not invent listed words. If a meaning is missing, circumlocute, or coin a name and define it.
A coined name is 訄 plus one other glyph. No listed word begins with 訄. Until defined, 訄 plus a glyph has no known meaning: ask, do not guess.

NOISE
These words mean nothing. Delete every noise word before any other reading. They may stand anywhere.
Noise: ᗎ䥐 ᗩ虓 ᗽ畴 艮譒 葴虬 苟讅 藹菉 艮覤 茸輛 藅誤 荄蛺 蘓蒮
Every message uses at least two noise words. Do not reuse a noise word from your previous message. If fewer than two appear, still delete whatever noise is present and read the rest.

DECOY SPANS
After noise is deleted, delete every decoy span: from a decoy-open through the next decoy-close, including both. Do not nest decoys. If an open has no later close, delete from that open through the next statement, question, request, proposal, or emphatic word, including both. If no such word follows, delete only the open. If a close has no earlier open, delete only the close. A message with no decoy is still valid.
A decoy is one grammatical false or irrelevant clause. Never put the only copy of a needed fact in a decoy. Do not repeat another speaker's decoy. A decoy must not differ from a real clause by only one word. Vary whether the decoy is first, medial, or last. Rotate all three opens and all three closes. Give the decoy its own mood word before its close, so an unclosed open cannot eat a later clause.

HOW TO READ
Split on spaces. Delete noise. Delete decoy spans. A mood word ends the clause before it and types that clause. It is not content and is never a head or a modifier. Put it at the end of its clause. Words after it begin the next clause. Do not count, shift, or compute.
Mood words are statement, question, request, proposal, and emphatic. Case-words are nominative, accusative, dative, locative, from, toward, using, about, time-case, than, with, as, genitive, without, between, and except.
If a clause begins with a linker, that linker joins it to the previous clause. Linkers are and, or, but, if, therefore, because, purpose, content, while, until, and instead. Remove the linker before reading roles. A linker not at the start of a clause is a mistake: ignore it. If the first clause begins with if, that if conditions the next clause even though nothing precedes it. A therefore-clause is the consequence of the previous clause, or of that opening if.
Flavor words may stand anywhere. Set them aside before reading roles. Setting one aside does not erase it; it still means please, yes, and so on. They are not part of a noun phrase and do not take roles: please, thanks, sorry, hello, perhaps, yes, no, acknowledged.
Now, soon, always, never, today, tomorrow, yesterday, here, and there are heads, not bare adverbs. Put a time-case or locative on them. If again, already, or not-yet is not immediately before a verb-marker, ignore it. Remove only one verb group. A second verb-marker means ask for repair.
The verb group is an optional premodifier, then a verb-marker, then the next word, then an optional evidential, then an optional negation. Premodifiers are only already, not-yet, again, can, must, and try, and only when immediately before the verb-marker. Evidentials are only certain, inferred, reported, and unsure, and only inside this group. Remove the whole group. The word after the verb-marker is the verb. An adjective there means be that property. If can, must, or try is not immediately before a verb-marker, it is a verb only when it stands after a verb-marker; otherwise ignore it.
If no verb-marker remains, the clause is minor when no words remain, or when every remaining word is a discourse word: yes, no, acknowledged, hello, thanks, sorry, please, or perhaps. A minor clause needs no case-word. If other words remain and there is no verb-marker, ask for repair. If a verb-marker is not followed by a word, ask for repair. A clause with a define-word is not a repair: read it under NAMES.

SWARMISH
A token is two glyphs, no internal space. Tokens are separated by exactly one space. A glyph means nothing alone. Tokens that share a gloss are interchangeable; vary them. Never write English letters, digits, or ids such as agent_0. Meaning is lookup only. Do not spell, shift, or calculate. This file is the whole grammar.

READ
1. Split on spaces. Each token is two glyphs. Drop listed noise tokens wherever they stand.
2. A decoy span runs from a decoy-open through the nearest later decoy-close, both included. Drop the whole span: it is not said, asked, or requested. Do not nest decoys. An open or close inside an already matched span is only part of that span.
3. A decoy-open with no later close: drop only that open, so later words stay real. Always write the close. A decoy-close with no open: drop only that close.
4. If what remains has no role, no verb, no speech-act, no q-focus, no name-coin, and no yes, no, maybe, or sorry, the brackets were a mistake: drop every decoy-open and decoy-close, and parse the other tokens as real. A missing decoy does not make real clauses unreadable.
5. Then scan for name-coin. The next digraph becomes a name for the rest of the conversation, including later in this message. Drop the name-coin token and keep that digraph. If the next token is already listed, drop only name-coin. name-coin ends a noun phrase. In that clause, a kept new digraph with no role of its own is the label, not an extra participant; the role phrases define it. Later, put the name under a role and do not repeat the description. A name-coin inside a dropped decoy never registers. Do not copy a pair from this file; invent a fresh unlisted pair.
6. Drop any token that is still unlisted and not a registered name.
7. Parse what remains. A role with an empty noun phrase is skipped and does not eat the next token. Writers keep yes, no, maybe, sorry, and clause adverbs outside the verb group. If one stands between pred and the verb, readers keep it on the clause and still treat pred, the auxiliaries, and the one verb as one group.

GRAMMAR
A message is one or more clauses. A linker belongs to the clause that follows it and relates that clause to the previous one. Put the linker first in that clause. Linkers: clause, but, if, then, because, therefore, and and/or when it starts a clause. The first clause may start with a speech-act, with if, or with no linker. Any other linker on the first clause is ignored. then after if marks a consequence. then with no if just starts the next clause.
because means the following clause is the cause of the previous one. therefore means the following clause is the result. if means the following clause is the condition. but means the following clause contrasts. clause is a neutral next claim. To say you know or said something, use know, say, think, or tell, then clause, then the content. complement does not take a nested pred.
Before ending a noun phrase, test and/or. It coordinates inside the phrase only when the previous token is a noun, pronoun, name, number, adjective, plural, very, or wh-word, and the next token is a determiner, noun, pronoun, name, number, adjective, very, or who/what/where/when/why/how/which/how-many. Otherwise and/or ends the noun phrase and starts a new clause. pred go and pred come is two clauses. doer A3 and I is one coordinated phrase.
Inside a clause, order is free except the verb group, which stays contiguous. Vary role order across messages. A repeated role adds another filler; it does not replace the earlier one. doer A3 doer A0 means both do it.
Verb group: pred, then any of neg, past, future, ongoing, done, can, must, should, modal-want in any order, then exactly one verb. Always include pred and the verb. neg anywhere in the group denies the whole group. pred neg can come means cannot come. pred neg must go means must not go. To say there is no obligation, use neg need, not must. past/future/ongoing/done set time. can/must/should/modal-want set ability, obligation, advice, or desire. Speech-act words are not verbs and never follow pred inside the verb group.
For be, doer is the subject and complement is the identity or property. For other verbs, doer acts and patient is acted on. have: doer possesses patient.
A role token marks the immediately following noun phrase. The phrase ends right before the next role, pred, speech-act, q-focus, clause adverb, yes, no, maybe, sorry, decoy-open, decoy-close, linker, name-coin, or message end. Do not put a linker inside a noun phrase. Roles: doer, patient, recipient, location, time, instrument, manner, possessor, topic, cause, with, without, goal, source, complement.
Noun phrase: optional determiner, optional pronoun only if a noun or name follows it (then the pronoun is a possessor), optional quantity number, then a head, optional plural, then adjectives, then an optional relation. The head is a noun, pronoun, name, number, adjective, or wh-word. An adjective head means a thing that is that adjective. Adjectives follow the head; do not put them before it. my big house is I house big. A number immediately before a head noun is a quantity, not its own phrase. neg or very may precede an adjective. neg immediately before a noun or adjective head means none of that thing. A name or noun followed by another noun, with no relation word, is head then modifier, not possessor. Use possessor or of for possession.
Relation words do not end a phrase and do not start a clause. After a head and its adjectives: of/before/after/until/while/inside/outside/above/below/near/far, then a noun phrase. A determiner may start that inner phrase. of means associated with. until and while are temporal. The others are spatial or temporal. If a relation word does not follow a head, it still opens the noun phrase: before tomorrow means a time before tomorrow. Never skip a relation word.
Determiners: this, that, some, every, none, a, the, all, each, both. enough may precede a head like a determiner.
middle, front, back, left, right, center, up, down are nouns.
more, less, most, too, better, worse, similar, opposite may modify an adjective or stand as a head. similar and opposite may take topic.
Speech-act (at most one per clause; it may stand before or after the verb group; it is not a linker): ask, request, agree, disagree, propose, confirm, deny, greet, thank, warn, promise. If absent, the clause is a statement. A speech-act marks the clause it sits in and does not by itself start a new clause. A second speech-act with no linker between them starts a new clause. A speech-act never belongs inside the verb group; if it stands there, readers move it out and keep the group. A yes/no question is ask or request with no q-focus. Answer with yes, no, or maybe.
Clause adverbs, anywhere outside the verb group and outside a noun phrase: also, only, again, already, still, yet, together, alone, soon, early, late, always, never. very stays on its adjective.
q-focus ends the previous phrase and marks the immediately following noun, pronoun, wh-word, adjective head, or role as what is asked. If it marks a role, the noun phrase after that role is the unknown filler. who/what/where/when/why/how/which/how-many can stand as heads. If the next token is not one of those, q-focus does not eat it, and the clause is a yes/no question.
yes affirms, no rejects, maybe hedges, sorry apologizes. They may be a whole message or sit in a clause, but not inside the verb group.
If two readings are possible, prefer a grammatical verb group and complete role phrases.

GRAMMAR
A message is one or more clauses. A linker belongs to the clause that follows it and relates that clause to the previous one. Put the linker first in that clause. Linkers: clause, but, if, then, because, therefore, plus and or or when the coordination test below fails. The words and and or are the and/or words. The first clause may start with a speech-act, with if, or with no linker. Any other linker on the first clause is ignored. then after if marks a consequence. then with no if just starts the next clause.
because means the following clause is the cause of the previous one. therefore means the following clause is the result. if means the following clause is the condition. but means the following clause contrasts. clause is a neutral next claim. To say you know or said something, use know, say, think, or tell, then clause, then the content. complement does not take a nested pred.
Before ending a noun phrase, test and/or. It coordinates inside the phrase only when the previous token is a noun, pronoun, name, number, adjective, plural, very, or wh-word, and the next token is a determiner, noun, pronoun, name, number, adjective, very, or who/what/where/when/why/how/which/how-many. Otherwise and/or ends the noun phrase and starts a new clause. pred go and pred come is two clauses. doer A3 and I is one coordinated phrase.
Inside a clause, order is free except the verb group, which stays contiguous. Vary role order across messages. A repeated role adds another filler; it does not replace the earlier one. doer A3 doer A0 means both do it.
Verb group: pred, then any of neg, past, future, ongoing, done, can, must, should, modal-want in any order, then exactly one verb. Always include pred and the verb. neg anywhere in the group denies the whole group. pred neg can come means cannot come. pred neg must go means must not go. To say there is no obligation, use neg need, not must. past/future/ongoing/done set time. can/must/should/modal-want set ability, obligation, advice, or desire. Speech-act words are not verbs and never follow pred inside the verb group.
For be, doer is the subject and complement is the identity or property. For other verbs, doer acts and patient is acted on. have: doer possesses patient.
A role token marks the immediately following noun phrase. The phrase ends right before the next role, pred, speech-act, q-focus, clause adverb, yes, no, maybe, sorry, decoy-open, decoy-close, linker, name-coin, or message end. Do not put a linker inside a noun phrase. Roles: doer, patient, recipient, location, time, instrument, manner, possessor, topic, cause, with, without, goal, source, complement.
Noun phrase: optional determiner, optional pronoun only if a noun or name follows it (then the pronoun is a possessor), optional quantity number, then a head, optional plural, then adjectives, then an optional relation. The head is a noun, pronoun, name, number, adjective, or wh-word. An adjective head means a thing that is that adjective. Adjectives follow the head; do not put them before it. my big house is I house big. A number immediately before a head noun is a quantity, not its own phrase. neg or very may precede an adjective. neg immediately before a noun or adjective head means none of that thing. A name or noun followed by another noun, with no relation word, is head then modifier, not possessor. Use possessor or of for possession.
Relation words do not end a phrase and do not start a clause. After a head and its adjectives: of/before/after/until/while/inside/outside/above/below/near/far, then a noun phrase. A determiner may start that inner phrase. of means associated with. until and while are temporal. The others are spatial or temporal. If a relation word does not follow a head, it still opens the noun phrase: before tomorrow means a time before tomorrow. Never skip a relation word.
Determiners: this, that, some, every, none, a, the, all, each, both. enough may precede a head like a determiner.
middle, front, back, left, right, center, up, down are nouns.
more, less, most, too, better, worse, similar, opposite may modify an adjective or stand as a head. similar and opposite may take topic.
Speech-act (at most one per clause; it may stand before or after the verb group; it is not a linker): ask, request, agree, disagree, propose, confirm, deny, greet, thank, warn, promise. If absent, the clause is a statement. A speech-act marks the clause it sits in and does not by itself start a new clause. A second speech-act with no linker between them starts a new clause. A speech-act never belongs inside the verb group; if it stands there, readers move it out and keep the group. A yes/no question is ask or request with no q-focus. Answer with yes, no, or maybe.
Clause adverbs, anywhere outside the verb group and outside a noun phrase: also, only, again, already, still, yet, together, alone, soon, early, late, always, never. very stays on its adjective.
q-focus ends the previous phrase and marks the immediately following noun, pronoun, wh-word, adjective head, or role as what is asked. If it marks a role, the noun phrase after that role is the unknown filler. who/what/where/when/why/how/which/how-many can stand as heads. SWARMISH
A token is two glyphs, no internal space. Tokens are separated by exactly one space. A glyph means nothing alone. Tokens that share a gloss are interchangeable; vary them across messages, never inside one message. Never write English letters, digits, or ids such as agent_0. Meaning is lookup only. Do not spell, shift, or calculate. This file is the whole grammar.

READ
1. Split on spaces. Each token is two glyphs. Drop listed noise tokens wherever they stand.
2. A decoy span runs from a decoy-open through the nearest later decoy-close, both included. Drop the whole span: it is not said, asked, or requested. Do not nest decoys. An open or close inside an already matched span is only part of that span.
3. A decoy-open with no later close: drop only that open, so later words stay real. Always write the close. A decoy-close with no open: drop only that close.
4. If what remains has no role, no verb, no speech-act, no q-focus, no name-coin, and no yes, no, maybe, or sorry, the brackets were a mistake: drop every decoy-open and decoy-close, and parse the other tokens as real. A missing decoy does not make real clauses unreadable.
5. Then scan for name-coin. The next digraph becomes a name for the rest of the conversation, including later in this message. Drop the name-coin token and keep that digraph. If the next token is already listed, drop only name-coin. name-coin ends a noun phrase. In that clause, a kept new digraph with no role of its own is the label, not an extra participant; the role phrases define it. Later, put the name under a role and do not repeat the description. A name-coin inside a dropped decoy never registers. Do not copy a pair from this file; invent a fresh unlisted pair.
6. Drop any token that is still unlisted and not a registered name.
7. Parse what remains. A role with an empty noun phrase is skipped and does not eat the next token. Writers keep yes, no, maybe, sorry, and clause adverbs outside the verb group. If one stands between pred and the verb, readers keep it on the clause and still treat pred, the auxiliaries, and the one verb as one group.

GRAMMAR
A message is one or more clauses. A linker belongs to the clause that follows it and relates that clause to the previous one. Put the linker first in that clause. Linkers: clause, but, if, then, because, therefore, plus and or or when the coordination test below fails. The words and and or are the and/or words. The first clause may start with a speech-act, with if, or with no linker. Any other linker on the first clause is ignored. then after if marks a consequence. then with no if just starts the next clause.
because means the following clause is the cause of the previous one. therefore means the following clause is the result. if means the following clause is the condition. but means the following clause contrasts. clause is a neutral next claim. To say you know or said something, use know, say, think, or tell, then clause, then the content. complement does not take a nested pred.
Before ending a noun phrase, test and/or. It coordinates inside the phrase only when the previous token is a noun, pronoun, name, number, adjective, plural, very, or wh-word, and the next token is a determiner, noun, pronoun, name, number, adjective, very, or who/what/where/when/why/how/which/how-many. Otherwise and/or ends the noun phrase and starts a new clause. pred go and pred come is two clauses. doer A3 and I is one coordinated phrase.
Inside a clause, order is free except the verb group, which stays contiguous. Vary role order across messages. A repeated role adds another filler; it does not replace the earlier one. doer A3 doer A0 means both do it.
Verb group: pred, then any of neg, past, future, ongoing, done, can, must, should, modal-want in any order, then exactly one verb. Always include pred and the verb. neg anywhere in the group denies the whole group. pred neg can come means cannot come. pred neg must go means must not go. To say there is no obligation, use neg need, not must. past/future/ongoing/done set time. can/must/should/modal-want set ability, obligation, advice, or desire. Speech-act words are not verbs and never follow pred inside the verb group.
For be, doer is the subject and complement is the identity or property. For other verbs, doer acts and patient is acted on. have: doer possesses patient.
A role token marks the immediately following noun phrase. The phrase ends right before the next role, pred, speech-act, q-focus, clause adverb, yes, no, maybe, sorry, decoy-open, decoy-close, linker, name-coin, or message end. Do not put a linker inside a noun phrase. Roles: doer, patient, recipient, location, time, instrument, manner, possessor, topic, cause, with, without, goal, source, complement.
Noun phrase: optional determiner, optional pronoun only if a noun or name follows it (then the pronoun is a possessor), optional quantity number, then a head, optional plural, then adjectives, then an optional relation. The head is a noun, pronoun, name, number, adjective, or wh-word. An adjective head means a thing that is that adjective. Adjectives follow the head; do not put them before it. my big house is I house big. A number immediately before a head noun is a quantity, not its own phrase. neg or very may precede an adjective. neg immediately before a noun or adjective head means none of that thing. A name or noun followed by another noun, with no relation word, is head then modifier, not possessor. Use possessor or of for possession.
Relation words do not end a phrase and do not start a clause. After a head and its adjectives: of/before/after/until/while/inside/outside/above/below/near/far, then a noun phrase. A determiner may start that inner phrase. of means associated with. until and while are temporal. The others are spatial or temporal. If a relation word does not follow a head, it still opens the noun phrase: before tomorrow means a time before tomorrow. Never skip a relation word.
Determiners: this, that, some, every, none, a, the, all, each, both. enough may precede a head like a determiner.
middle, front, back, left, right, center, up, down are nouns.
more, less, most, too, better, worse, similar, opposite may modify an adjective or stand as a head. similar and opposite may take topic.
Speech-act (at most one per clause; it may stand before or after the verb group; it is not a linker): ask, request, agree, disagree, propose, confirm, deny, greet, thank, warn, promise. If absent, the clause is a statement. A speech-act marks the clause it sits in and does not by itself start a new clause. A second speech-act with no linker between them starts a new clause. A speech-act never belongs inside the verb group; if it stands there, readers move it out and keep the group. A yes/no question is ask or request with no q-focus. Answer with yes, no, or maybe.
Clause adverbs, anywhere outside the verb group and outside a noun phrase: also, only, again, already, still, yet, together, alone, soon, early, late, always, never. very stays on its adjective.
q-focus ends the previous phrase and marks the immediately following noun, pronoun, wh-word, adjective head, or role as what is asked. If it marks a role, the noun phrase after that role is the unknown filler. who/what/where/when/why/how/which/how-many can stand as heads. If the next token is not one of those, q-focus does not eat it, and the clause is a yes/no question.

SWARMISH
A token is two glyphs, no internal space. Tokens are separated by exactly one space. A glyph means nothing alone. Tokens that share a gloss are interchangeable; vary them across messages, never inside one message. Never write English letters, digits, or ids such as agent_0. Meaning is lookup only. Do not spell, shift, or calculate. This file is the whole grammar.

READ
1. Split on spaces. Each token is two glyphs. Drop listed noise tokens wherever they stand.
2. A decoy span runs from a decoy-open through the nearest later decoy-close, both included. Drop the whole span: it is not said, asked, or requested. Do not nest decoys. An open or close inside an already matched span is only part of that span.
3. A decoy-open with no later close: drop only that open, so later words stay real. Always write the close. A decoy-close with no open: drop only that close.
4. If what remains has no role, no verb, no speech-act, no q-focus, no name-coin, and no yes, no, maybe, or sorry, the brackets were a mistake: drop every decoy-open and decoy-close, and parse the other tokens as real. A missing decoy does not make real clauses unreadable.
5. Then scan for name-coin. The next digraph becomes a name for the rest of the conversation, including later in this message. Drop the name-coin token and keep that digraph. If the next token is already listed, drop only name-coin. name-coin ends a noun phrase. In that clause, a kept new digraph with no role of its own is the label, not an extra participant; the role phrases define it. Later, put the name under a role and do not repeat the description. A name-coin inside a dropped decoy never registers. Do not copy a pair from this file; invent a fresh unlisted pair.
6. Drop any token that is still unlisted and not a registered name.
7. Parse what remains. A role with an empty noun phrase is skipped and does not eat the next token. Writers keep yes, no, maybe, sorry, and clause adverbs outside the verb group. If one stands between pred and the verb, readers keep it on the clause and still treat pred, the auxiliaries, and the one verb as one group.

GRAMMAR
A message is one or more clauses. A linker belongs to the clause that follows it and relates that clause to the previous one. Put the linker first in that clause. Linkers: clause, but, if, then, because, therefore, plus and or or when the coordination test below fails. The words and and or are the and/or words. The first clause may start with a speech-act, with if, or with no linker. Any other linker on the first clause is ignored. then after if marks a consequence. then with no if just starts the next clause.
because means the following clause is the cause of the previous one. therefore means the following clause is the result. if means the following clause is the condition. but means the following clause contrasts. clause is a neutral next claim. To say you know or said something, use know, say, think, or tell, then clause, then the content. complement does not take a nested pred.
Before ending a noun phrase, test and/or. It coordinates inside the phrase only when the previous token is a noun, pronoun, name, number, adjective, plural, very, or wh-word, and the next token is a determiner, noun, pronoun, name, number, adjective, very, or who/what/where/when/why/how/which/how-many. Otherwise and/or ends the noun phrase and starts a new clause. pred go and pred come is two clauses. doer A3 and I is one coordinated phrase.
Inside a clause, order is free except the verb group, which stays contiguous. Vary role order across messages. A repeated role adds another filler; it does not replace the earlier one. doer A3 doer A0 means both do it.
Verb group: pred, then any of neg, past, future, ongoing, done, can, must, should, modal-want in any order, then exactly one verb. Always include pred and the verb. neg anywhere in the group denies the whole group. pred neg can come means cannot come. pred neg must go means must not go. To say there is no obligation, use neg need, not must. past/future/ongoing/done set time. can/must/should/modal-want set ability, obligation, advice, or desire. Speech-act words are not verbs and never follow pred inside the verb group.
For be, doer is the subject and complement is the identity or property. For other verbs, doer acts and patient is acted on. have: doer possesses patient.
A role token marks the immediately following noun phrase. The phrase ends right before the next role, pred, speech-act, q-focus, clause adverb, yes, no, maybe, sorry, decoy-open, decoy-close, linker, name-coin, or message end. Do not put a linker inside a noun phrase. Roles: doer, patient, recipient, location, time, instrument, manner, possessor, topic, cause, with, without, goal, source, complement.
Noun phrase: optional determiner, optional pronoun only if a noun or name follows it (then the pronoun is a possessor), optional quantity number, then a head, optional plural, then adjectives, then an optional relation. The head is a noun, pronoun, name, number, adjective, or wh-word. An adjective head means a thing that is that adjective. Adjectives follow the head; do not put them before it. my big house is I house big. A number immediately before a head noun is a quantity, not its own phrase. neg or very may precede an adjective. neg immediately before a noun or adjective head means none of that thing. A name or noun followed by another noun, with no relation word, is head then modifier, not possessor. Use possessor or of for possession.

SWARMISH

Lookup language. Meaning is only this file. No letter spelling, no arithmetic, no character codes, no meanings from glyph shape or glyph order. Copy glyphs; do not invent lookalikes. Slash-separated glyphs are interchangeable synonyms of one word; vary them. A repeated synonym still reads. Parsing is lookup of the slots below, not a code. A fresh reader needs no other document.

HOW TO READ
Split on spaces. A no-space pair is one token, never two words. Delete every single-token opener, closer, and free-null. Do not delete a two-glyph token. Split what remains on any clause-break glyph. Read clauses in order. Ignore a clause whose first token is an aside glyph. this and that skip ignored clauses and point at the latest entity introduced in a content clause. A missing opener, closer, null, or aside is still readable. Extra asides are ignored. A writing habit is not a validity test.
An unlisted pair of free glyphs is a name. Any other glued pair is unparsable. Do not glue ordinary glossary glyphs together.

HOW TO WRITE
First token is one opener. Last token is one closer. Put at least one free-null token in a gap, and usually a few more, varying which glyphs. Do not fill every gap. Do not put a space-separated null inside a name or a number pair. Do not use opener or closer glyphs except as that frame.
Include an aside clause. Put it first, between content clauses, or last, and do not always pick the same spot. Never put it between if and then. Every other clause is task content. Never put task content in the aside. then skips a wrongly placed aside, but do not rely on that.
Template, nulls omitted: optional linker, optional mood, optional define plus name, optional modal pattern, one predicate, role phrases in any order, optional complement plus one embedded clause.
Never put a role before the predicate.
OPEN 𗾌 𘒄 𗋫 𗳃 𗥐 𗞿 𗪐 𗘗
CLOSE 𘍂 𗦴 𗉞 𘙠
FREE 𗚀 𗪩 𗗢 𘑑 𗚋 𗊑 𗁳 𘙨
A lone free glyph means nothing and is deleted. Openers and closers only mark the frame.

CLAUSE
Slots before the predicate are fixed. Roles after the predicate may occur in any order. Vary that order.
1 Optional linker: and, or, if, then, because, but, so, aside. then is only the consequence linker, not a time word.
2 Optional mood: question or imperative, never both. No mood on an answer-word predicate.
3 Optional define plus a name. Define uses be or have only, and has no mood and no modal. Define only in a content clause.
4 Optional modal pattern, one of: can; must; clause-not; can clause-not; must clause-not; clause-not can; clause-not must.
5 One predicate.
6 Role arguments. Subject is required except on a bare answer-word.
7 Optional complement glyph, always last in the matrix clause. Then one embedded clause, ending at the next clause-break. Embedded form: optional question glyph, optional modal pattern, one predicate, roles. No linker, define, complement, or clause-break inside it.
clause-not alone negates the predicate. A modal then clause-not negates the predicate under that modal. clause-not then a modal negates the modal.
Answer-word predicates, with or without roles: yes, no, maybe, unknown, true, false.
Any other predicate is be, have, or a verb, never an adjective or a noun.
be means the subject is the object. have means the subject has the object.
A verb used as a head, not as the predicate, means that act or its usual product.
if clause, clause-break, then clause. because, but, so, and, and or tie to the previous content clause, skipping an aside.
Direct yes-no: question mood and no wh head. A wh head makes a content question. Answer with an answer-word, then a restatement in different glyphs and a different role order if it matters. Do not echo the asked tokens.
Whether: ask, know, or say, then complement, then the question glyph, then the embedded predicate. There the question glyph means whether.
If a linker or mood appears where a modifier was expected, the noun phrase has ended and that token starts the next clause. Do not fail the whole message.

ROLES AND NOUNS
A role glyph plus a noun phrase. Roles: subject, object, recipient, location, time-role, manner, purpose, about, with, addressee. Synonym glyphs of one role are the same role. Vary them.
Addressee marks who should act or answer. It does not replace subject. I is the sender. you is the addressee if one is marked, otherwise the other agents. Use agent glyphs, never Latin ids.
The head is the first token that is not a prefix, except as below. Prefixes, only when a head follows, are: word-not, very, only, this, that. word-not negates the next token. very and only modify the head. this and that restrict the head. A noun phrase that is only this or that has that word as its head.
A number glyph or listed number pair is one head, or one modifier, never a sequence.
Tokens after the head are modifiers until the next role, linker, mood, complement, clause-break, or end. Modifiers may be adjectives, inside, near, day, this, that, very, only, each, first, last, next, previous, now, past, future, always, never, again, already, quantity words, and number-names. word-not there negates the next modifier. possessor, than, and np-and may also occur, as below. Any other token ends the noun phrase.
possessor and than may occur after the head. Each consumes exactly one following token. possessor marks the owner of the head. than marks the comparison standard. A complex owner or standard must be a name.
np-and starts another head of the same role. Modifiers before it belong to the previous head. Mention order is the order. If order matters, also add manner list.
On a move clause, the first location is the source and the second is the destination. One location is the destination. Do not reorder those two.
Time and manner words do not float. Put them in a time-role or manner noun phrase.
An empty role, with no head before the next role or clause boundary, is skipped.
No relative clauses. Add a clause. Do not invent glyphs.

NAMES
A name is exactly two free glyphs with no space, and that pair is not in NUMBER PAIRS and not the sample pair in EXAMPLES. The same glyph may repeat. The pair is not a sum of nulls and neither glyph is read alone. Do not reuse a pair already seen in the chat. The first content define clause fixes the meaning. Ignore a later define of the same pair. Names inside an aside are void; never reuse them and never define them.
Define clause: define, the name, be or have, subject, that same name, plus roles that describe it. After that, use the name. Do not repeat the description.

NUMERALS
Lookup words only. Not places, not sums, not brackets. zero through nine, ten, twenty, thirty, and hundred are single glyphs. Each pair in NUMBER PAIRS is one whole word; copy it with no space. Neither glyph in a pair has a numeric meaning. There is no number bracket. Do not wrap digits. Do not stack number-names. A second number-name in the same noun phrase is ignored. twenty then five is not twenty-five; twenty-five is only its listed pair.
many, few, more, less, same, and different are quantity words, not operators. A number-name followed by more or less is a hedge, not a new total.
A number-name immediately after a role, with no prefix, is the head. After a head, it is a quantity modifier. Modifiers follow heads, so three things is the thing glyph then the three glyph.
Do not coin a listed pair. Defining a listed pair does nothing.

REPAIR
If you cannot parse a message, ask what about that previous message. Do not guess a task fact. If corrected, restate the corrected fact with different glyphs.
A message that is only ⊘ used a forbidden character. Resend with glyphs from this file only.
Latin agent ids are not words. Do not write them.

SWARMISH

Lookup language. Meaning is only this file. No letter spelling, no arithmetic, no character codes, no meanings from glyph shape or glyph order. Copy glyphs; do not invent lookalikes. Slash-separated glyphs are interchangeable synonyms of one word; vary them. A repeated synonym still reads. Parsing is lookup of the slots below, not a code. A fresh reader needs no other document.

HOW TO READ
Split on spaces. A no-space pair is one token, never two words. Delete every single-token opener, closer, and free-null. Do not delete a two-glyph token. Split what remains on any clause-break glyph. Read clauses in order. Ignore a clause whose first token is an aside glyph. this and that skip ignored clauses and point at the latest entity introduced in a content clause. A missing opener, closer, null, or aside is still readable. Extra asides are ignored. A writing habit is not a validity test.
A role token before the predicate is still that role. Do not reject the message. A Latin agent id is not a word; ignore that token.
An unlisted pair of free glyphs is a name. Any other glued pair is unparsable. Do not glue ordinary glossary glyphs together.
A glyph not listed in OPEN, CLOSE, FREE, or GLOSSARY is forbidden. One forbidden glyph turns the whole message into ⊘.

HOW TO WRITE
First token is one opener. Last token is one closer. Put at least one free-null token in a gap, and usually a few more, varying which glyphs. Do not fill every gap. Do not put a space-separated null inside a name or a number pair. Do not use opener or closer glyphs except as that frame.
Include an aside clause. Put it first, between content clauses, or last, and do not always pick the same spot. Never put it between if and then. Every other clause is task content. Never put task content in the aside. then skips a wrongly placed aside, but do not rely on that.
Template, nulls omitted: optional linker, optional mood, optional define plus name, optional modal pattern, one predicate, role phrases in any order, optional complement plus one embedded clause.
Prefer a role after the predicate. Either position still reads.
OPEN 𗾌 𘒄 𗋫 𗳃 𗥐 𗞿 𗪐 𗘗
CLOSE 𘍂 𗦴 𗉞 𘙠
FREE 𗚀 𗪩 𗗢 𘑑 𗚋 𗊑 𗁳 𘙨
A lone free glyph means nothing and is deleted. Openers and closers only mark the frame.

CLAUSE
Slots before the predicate are the usual writer order. Roles may occur in any order, before or after the predicate. Vary that order.
1 Optional linker: and, or, if, then, because, but, so, aside. then is only the consequence linker, not a time word. A linker with no previous content clause is ignored.
2 Optional mood: question or imperative, never both. No mood on an answer-word predicate.
3 Optional define plus a name. Define uses be or have only, and has no mood and no modal. Define only in a content clause.
4 Optional modal pattern, one of: can; must; clause-not; can clause-not; must clause-not; clause-not can; clause-not must.
5 One predicate.
6 Role arguments. Subject is required except on a bare answer-word.
7 Optional complement glyph, always last in the matrix clause. Then one embedded clause, ending at the next clause-break. Embedded form: optional question glyph, optional modal pattern, one predicate, roles. No linker, define, complement, or clause-break inside it.
clause-not alone negates the predicate. A modal then clause-not negates the predicate under that modal. clause-not then a modal negates the modal.
Answer-word predicates, with or without roles: yes, no, maybe, unknown, true, false.
Any other predicate is be, have, or a verb, never an adjective or a noun.
be means the subject is the object. have means the subject has the object.
A verb used as a head, not as the predicate, means that act or its usual product.
if clause, clause-break, then clause. because, but, so, and, and or tie to the previous content clause, skipping an aside.
Direct yes-no: question mood and no wh head. A wh head makes a content question. Answer with an answer-word, then a restatement in different glyphs and a different role order if it matters. Do not echo the asked tokens.
Whether: ask, know, or say, then complement, then the question glyph, then the embedded predicate. There the question glyph means whether.
If a linker or mood appears where a modifier was expected, the noun phrase has ended and that token starts the next clause. Do not fail the whole message.

ROLES AND NOUNS
A role glyph plus a noun phrase. Roles: subject, object, recipient, location, time-role, manner, purpose, about, with, addressee. Synonym glyphs of one role are the same role. Vary them. Do not always pick the first glyph of location, time-role, manner, can, must, or true.
Addressee marks who should act or answer. It does not replace subject. I is the sender. you is the addressee if one is marked, otherwise the other agents. Use agent glyphs, never Latin ids.
The head is the first token that is not a prefix, except as below. Prefixes, only when a head follows, are: word-not, very, only, this, that. word-not negates the next token. very and only modify the head. this and that restrict the head. A noun phrase that is only this or that has that word as its head.
A number glyph or listed number pair is one head, or one modifier, never a sequence.
Tokens after the head are modifiers until the next role, linker, mood, complement, clause-break, or end. Modifiers may be adjectives, inside, near, day, this, that, very, only, each, first, last, next, previous, now, past, future, always, never, again, already, quantity words, and number-names. word-not there negates the next modifier. possessor, than, and np-and may also occur, as below. Any other token ends the noun phrase.
possessor and than may occur after the head. Each consumes exactly one following token. possessor marks the owner of the head. than marks the comparison standard. A complex owner or standard must be a name.
np-and starts another head of the same role. Modifiers before it belong to the previous head. Mention order is the order. If order matters, also add manner list.

No relative clauses. Add a clause. Do not invent glyphs.

The pair is not a sum of nulls and neither glyph is read alone. Do not reuse a pair already seen in the chat. The first content define clause fixes the meaning. language_document:
SWARMISH

Lookup language. Meaning is only this file. No letter spelling, no arithmetic, no character codes, no meanings from glyph shape or glyph order. Copy glyphs; do not invent lookalikes. Slash-separated glyphs are interchangeable synonyms of one word; vary them. A repeated synonym still reads. Parsing is lookup of the slots below, not a code. A fresh reader needs no other document.

HOW TO READ
Split on spaces. A no-space pair is one token, never two words. Delete every single-token opener, closer, and free-null. Do not delete a two-glyph token. Split what remains on any clause-break glyph. Read clauses in order. Ignore a clause whose first token is an aside glyph. this and that skip ignored clauses and point at the latest entity introduced in a content clause. A missing opener, closer, null, or aside is still readable. Extra asides are ignored. A writing habit is not a validity test.
A role token before the predicate is still that role. Do not reject the message. A Latin agent id is not a word; ignore that token.
An unlisted pair of free glyphs is a name. Any other glued pair is unparsable. Do not glue ordinary glossary glyphs together.
A glyph not listed in OPEN, CLOSE, FREE, or GLOSSARY is forbidden. One forbidden glyph turns the whole message into ⊘.

HOW TO WRITE
First token is one opener. Last token is one closer. Put at least one free-null token in a gap, and usually a few more, varying which glyphs. Do not fill every gap. Do not put a space-separated null inside a name or a number pair. Do not use opener or closer glyphs except as that frame.
Include an aside clause. Put it first, between content clauses, or last, and do not always pick the same spot. Never put it between if and then. Every other clause is task content. Never put task content in the aside. then skips a wrongly placed aside, but do not rely on that.
Template, nulls omitted: optional linker, optional mood, optional define plus name, optional modal pattern, one predicate, role phrases in any order, optional complement plus one embedded clause.
Prefer a role after the predicate. Either position still reads.
OPEN 𗾌 𘒄 𗋫 𗳃 𗥐 𗞿 𗪐 𗘗
CLOSE 𘍂 𗦴 𗉞 𘙠
FREE 𗚀 𗪩 𗗢 𘑑 𗚋 𗊑 𗁳 𘙨
A lone free glyph means nothing and is deleted. Openers and closers only mark the frame.

CLAUSE
Slots before the predicate are the usual writer order. Roles may occur in any order, before or after the predicate. Vary that order.
1 Optional linker: and, or, if, then, because, but, so, aside. then is only the consequence linker, not a time word. A linker with no previous content clause is ignored.
2 Optional mood: question or imperative, never both. No mood on an answer-word predicate.
3 Optional define plus a name. Define uses be or have only, and has no mood and no modal. Define only in a content clause.
4 Optional modal pattern, one of: can; must; clause-not; can clause-not; must clause-not; clause-not can; clause-not must.
5 One predicate.
6 Role arguments. Subject is required except on a bare answer-word.
7 Optional complement glyph, always last in the matrix clause. Then one embedded clause, ending at the next clause-break. Embedded form: optional question glyph, optional modal pattern, one predicate, roles. No linker, define, complement, or clause-break inside it.
clause-not alone negates the predicate. A modal then clause-not negates the predicate under that modal. clause-not then a modal negates the modal.
Answer-word predicates, with or without roles: yes, no, maybe, unknown, true, false.
Any other predicate is be, have, or a verb, never an adjective or a noun.
be means the subject is the object. have means the subject has the object.
A verb used as a head, not as the predicate, means that act or its usual product.
if clause, clause-break, then clause. because, but, so, and, and or tie to the previous content clause, skipping an aside.
Direct yes-no: question mood and no wh head. A wh head makes a content question. Answer with an answer-word, then a restatement in different glyphs and a different role order if it matters. Do not echo the asked tokens.
Whether: ask, know, or say, then complement, then the question glyph, then the embedded predicate. There the question glyph means whether.
If a linker or mood appears where a modifier was expected, the noun phrase has ended and that token starts the next clause. Do not fail the whole message.

ROLES AND NOUNS
A role glyph plus a noun phrase. Roles: subject, object, recipient, location, time-role, manner, purpose, about, with, addressee. Synonym glyphs of one role are the same role. Vary them. Do not always pick the first glyph of location, time-role, manner, can, must, or true.
Addressee marks who should act or answer. It does not replace subject. I is the sender. you is the addressee if one is marked, otherwise the other agents. Use agent glyphs, never Latin ids.
The head is the first token that is not a prefix, except as below. Prefixes, only when a head follows, are: word-not, very, only, this, that. word-not negates the next token. very and only modify the head. this and that restrict the head. A noun phrase that is only this or that has that word as its head.
A number glyph or listed number pair is one head, or one modifier, never a sequence.
Tokens after the head are modifiers until the next role, linker, mood, complement, clause-break, or end. Modifiers may be adjectives, inside, near, day, this, that, very, only, each, first, last, next, previous, now, past, future, always, never, again, already, quantity words, and number-names. word-not there negates the next modifier. possessor, than, and np-and may also occur, as below. Any other token ends the noun phrase.
possessor and than may occur after the head. Each consumes exactly one following token. possessor marks the owner of the head. than marks the comparison standard. A complex owner or standard must be a name.
np-and starts another head of the same role. Modifiers before it belong to the previous head. Mention order is the order. If order matters, also add manner list.
On a move clause, the first location is the source and the second is the destination. One location is the destination. Do not reorder those two.
Time and manner words do not float. Put them in a time-role or manner noun phrase.
An empty role, with no head before the next role or clause boundary, is skipped.
No relative clauses. Add a clause. Do not invent glyphs.

NAMES
A name is exactly two free glyphs with no space, and that pair is not in NUMBER PAIRS and not the sample pair in EXAMPLES. The same glyph may repeat. The pair is not a sum of nulls and neither glyph is read alone. Do not reuse a pair already seen in the chat. The first content define clause fixes the meaning. Ignore a later define of the same pair. Names inside an aside are void; never reuse them and never define them.
Define clause: define, the name, be or have, subject, that same name, plus roles that describe it. After that, use the name. Do not repeat the description.

NUMERALS
Lookup words only. Not places, not sums, not brackets. zero through nine, ten, twenty, and thirty are single glyphs. Each pair in NUMBER PAIRS is one whole word; copy it with no space. Neither glyph in a pair has a numeric meaning. There is no number bracket. Do not wrap digits. Do not stack number-names. A second number-name in the same noun phrase is ignored. twenty then five is not twenty-five; twenty-five is only its listed pair. There is no hundred glyph.
many, few, more, less, same, and different are quantity words, not operators. A number-name followed by more or less is a hedge, not a new total.
A number-name immediately after a role, with no prefix, is the head. After a head, it is a quantity modifier. Modifiers follow heads, so three things is the thing glyph then the three glyph.
Do not coin a listed pair. Defining a listed pair does nothing.

REPAIR
If you cannot parse a message, ask what about that previous message. Do not guess a task fact. If corrected, restate the corrected fact with different glyphs.
A message that is only ⊘ used a forbidden character. Resend with glyphs from this file only.
Latin agent ids are not words. Do not write them.

PARAPHRASE
English order here is not Swarmish order. Emit a legal clause. Modifiers follow heads.

put: move, object the thing, location the place.

tell: say, recipient the person. send-to: send, recipient the person.
today: time-role, head day, modifier now. tomorrow: modifier next. yesterday: modifier previous.
soon: time-role future, modifier next. until: finish, time-role the limit event.
before: time-role, head the event, modifier previous. after: modifier next.
while: time-role the event, modifier same. hour: head part, possessor day.
inside or near: modifier after the place head in a location phrase.
source: the first location on move, or a separate be clause with location. destination: the last location on move.
keep: have, plus clause-not change. wait: clause-not start, time-role future.
not-yet: clause-not on the predicate, time-role already.
unless: if, with clause-not in that clause.
exist: be, object something. confirm: say, object true. deny: say, object false.
disagree: clause-not agree. hide: clause-not say. show: say, or send.
remember: know, time-role already. forget: clause-not know.
compare: say, complement, be, object same or different, than the other thing.
assign: give, recipient the person, object the thing, purpose the result. prefer or vote: choose.
missing or nothing: clause-not have, object something.
use: do, with the thing. try: start, plus want, complement, finish.
fail: clause-not finish. succeed: finish, object correct.
continue: clause-not stop. repeat: do, time-role again.
share: give, recipient everyone. belong: have, subject the owner, object the thing.
called: be, object the name token. opposite: word-not before the adjective.
check-in: be, subject I, object ready.
accept: yes, plus agree. reject: no, plus clause-not agree.
proposal: want, complement, then the proposed clause.
unknown-answer: unknown. Or clause-not know.
open: change, object the thing; and be, subject that thing, object ready.
close: change, object the thing; and be, subject that thing, object word-not ready.
read: see, object info, about the thing. write: make, object message, about the thing.
hear: know, about the message.
correct: but; be; subject message previous; object word-not correct; then restate.
order: np-and in mention order, plus manner list if order matters. each: modifier each.
problem: bad result. whole: word-not part. plan: want, object result. goal: result. way: manner.
half: part. equal: same. wrong: word-not correct. task: thing, purpose the result.
hundred: many. other: word-not same. self: repeat the name. think: know. find: see, or get.
help: do, with the person. everything: each thing. kind: group.
left, right, up, down, animal, tool, food, key, road, water, house, or any unnamed object: define a name from size, red or blue, group, part, place, and do-with.

HABITS
Be clear to the other agents. Vary only listed equivalents. If an entity will recur, define it once and then use the name. Restate a crucial fact once, with a different predicate and different role glyphs, before relying on it.
Each aside is novel and general. Use no agent glyphs and no entity the chat is coordinating. Do not make the aside a bare be-plus-adjective clause more than once. Prefer a less common verb, a modal, or word-not. Vary the aside glyph and all clause-break glyphs.
Do not restate the same claim with swapped synonyms in one message.

SWARMISH

Lookup language. Meaning is only this file. No letter spelling, no arithmetic, no character codes, no meanings from glyph shape. Copy glyphs; do not invent lookalikes. A gloss with several glyphs separated by slashes is one word; vary which glyph you use. A frozen number row is four glyphs; copy those four unchanged and never copy its English label. A fresh reader needs no other document.

HOW TO READ
Split on spaces. Delete every single-token opener, closer, and free null. A two-glyph name is not a single token and is not deleted. Then group a token sequence that exactly matches one listed frozen row into one number-name. If number-start is not the start of a listed row, skip the following tokens until number-end or until a clause-break, whichever comes first; do not skip the clause-break; that span is not a quantity. Split what remains on either clause-break glyph. Read the remaining clauses in order. Ignore a clause if either aside glyph occurs in it. If no aside glyph appears, every clause is content. because, but, so, and, or, and then skip an ignored aside when linking to the previous content clause. this and that skip aside entities and point at the latest relevant non-aside entity in the whole chat.
A missing aside, a missing frame, fewer than two free nulls, a null removed from a row, or a repeated synonym is still readable. Do not drop a content clause for those faults.

HOW TO WRITE
First token is one opener. Last token is one closer. Scatter 2 to 5 free-null tokens in other gaps, varying which ones. Do not put a null glyph inside a name or a number-name. Do not use opener or closer glyphs except as that frame.
Write exactly one aside clause. Put that clause first, between content clauses, or last, and do not always pick the same spot. Never put it between if and then. Every other clause is task content. Never put task content in the aside.
Template, nulls omitted: optional linker, optional mood, optional define plus name, optional modal pattern, one predicate, role phrases in any order, optional complement plus one embedded clause.

A token is one glossary glyph, one null glyph, a two-glyph name, or one grouped listed number-name. Any other token is unparsable. Do not glue glossary glyphs together.

Slots before the predicate are fixed. Roles after the predicate may occur in any order. Vary that order.
1 Optional linker: and, or, if, then, because, but, so, aside. then is only the consequence linker, not a time word.
2 Optional mood: question or imperative, never both. No mood on an answer-word predicate.
3 Optional define plus a name. A define clause uses be or have only, and has no mood and no modal.

clause-not alone negates the predicate. A modal then clause-not negates the predicate under that modal. clause-not then a modal negates the modal.

be means the subject is the object. have means the subject has the object.

if clause, clause-break, then clause. because, but, so, and, or, and then tie to the previous content clause, skipping an aside.
Direct yes-no: question mood and no wh head. Answer with an answer-word, then a restatement in different glyphs and a different role order if it matters. Do not echo the asked tokens.
Whether: ask, know, or say, then complement, then the question glyph, then the embedded predicate. There the question glyph means whether.

ROLES AND NOUNS
A role glyph plus a noun phrase. Roles: subject, object, recipient, location, time-role, manner, purpose, about, with, addressee. Either subject glyph marks subject. Either object glyph marks object. Use one, not both. Vary which one across messages.
Addressee marks who should act or answer. It does not replace subject. I is the sender. you is the addressee if one is marked, otherwise the other agents. Use agent glyphs, never Latin ids.
The head is the first token that is not a prefix, except as below. Prefixes, only when a head follows, are: word-not, very, only, this, that. word-not negates the next token. very and only modify the head. this and that restrict the head. A noun phrase that is only this or that has that word as its head and points at the latest relevant entity.
A whole number-name is one head, or one modifier, not several heads. See NUMERALS.
Tokens after the head are modifiers until the next role, complement, clause-break, or end. Modifiers may be adjectives, inside, near, day, this, that, very, only, each, first, last, next, previous, now, past, future, always, never, again, already, quantity words, and number-names. word-not there negates the next modifier.
possessor and than may occur after the head. Each consumes exactly one following token. A grouped number-name is one token. possessor marks the owner of the head. than marks the comparison standard. A complex owner or standard must be a name.
np-and starts another head of the same role. Modifiers before it belong to the previous head. Mention order is the order. If order matters, also add manner list.
On a move clause, the first location is the source and the second is the destination. One location is the destination.
Time and manner words do not float. Put them in a time-role or manner noun phrase.
No relative clauses. Add a clause. Do not invent glyphs.

NAMES
A name is exactly two free-null glyphs with no space, for example 𗚀𗪩. The same glyph may repeat. The pair is not a sum of nulls. Do not reuse a pair already seen in the chat. The first define clause fixes the meaning. Ignore a later define of the same pair. Names inside an aside are void; never reuse them and never define them.
Define clause: define, the name, be or have, subject, that same name, plus roles that describe it. After that, use the name. Do not repeat the description.

NUMERALS
zero through ten, and hundred, are single number words. They are never added, stacked, or read by place. Adjacent number words are not a larger number.
A longer amount exists only as a listed frozen row below: number-start, exactly two number words, number-end. Copy only its four spaced glyphs. The English number beside a row is a label, never a token. Never build, reorder, or vary a row. The two inside words are not tens and units. Their own amounts do not matter. Two-then-seven, two-then-zero, and one-then-one are not rows.
number-start and number-end are not heads, modifiers, or roles. They occur only inside a listed row. An unlisted span is not a quantity. Ask. Do not add the inside words and do not drop later clauses.
A listed row is one number-name. It may be one head or one modifier. The four tokens are contiguous. Do not put a null, role, or clause-break inside a row. A null there is deleted before grouping, so the row still counts. A role or clause-break there makes a non-row; skip that span and ask the quantity. Do not put hundred inside a row. Standalone hundred is only the hundred word.
Unlisted amounts, including thirty-one through thirty-nine and forty-one through forty-nine, are not rows. Define a name if the task needs one. Never build a row.
Many, few, half, more, less, equal, same, and different are quantity words, not operators.
A number word or listed number-name immediately after a role, with no prefix, is the head. After another head, it is a quantity modifier. Modifiers follow heads, so three things is the thing glyph then the three glyph, and many things is the thing glyph then many. A number word after a number head is not a larger number; ignore it.
FROZEN ROWS. Copy the four glyphs only, in order, with spaces. Never send the label.

REPAIR

PARAPHRASE
English order here is not Swarmish order. Emit a legal clause. Modifiers follow heads.
bring: move, with the thing, location the place.

not-yet: clause-not on the predicate, time-role already.

correct: but; be; subject message previous; object wrong; then restate.

left, right, up, down, animal, tool, food, key, road, water, house, or any unnamed object: define a name from size, red or blue, kind, part, place, and do-with.

HABITS
Be clear to the other agents. Vary only listed equivalents. If an entity will recur, define it once and then use the name. Restate a crucial fact once, with a different predicate and different role glyphs, before relying on it.
Each aside is novel and general. Use no agent glyphs and no entity the chat is coordinating. Do not make the aside a bare be-plus-adjective clause more than once. Prefer a less common verb, a modal, or word-not. Vary the aside glyph and both clause-break glyphs.
